docs.title: Planning
docs.text: RDM ships no planning tooling: tasks and issues live in their own tools (Plan vs. record).

docs.title: RDM
docs.text: RDM audits the record of regulated health software: the spec it is held to (written by whoever owns it, a factory such as Löyly or a team), the risks and the controls that reduce them, the checklists of the standards that apply, and the evidence that each requirement was verified. This glossary is the language of that record.

docs.title: Needs and requirements
docs.text:
Spec: What the product must do, written the Löyly way: a plan of slices (.pi/plan/), one per bounded context, each with its accepted Gherkin scenarios, its Allium model and its event model, and an event storm behind them. RDM's contract with a spec is only Gherkin and Allure, so plain feature files work too (spec: in the DHF's configuration). RDM reads it and never writes it. Avoid: design inputs, SDD, the record (for the spec alone)

User need: What an actor needs, as the spec captures it: a screen of a context's event model, with the Allium surface it links (whom it faces, the rules it provides, what it guarantees) and the event-storm events behind it (in plain Gherkin, a Feature, its description the need). It is validated, not verified. Avoid: user story, feature, epic, UN-n

Requirement: An accepted scenario of the spec, a concrete Given/When/Then example stamped with an id (@item-02-001; in plain Gherkin, any id-shaped tag): one acceptance criterion, accepted or not as a whole. It addresses the user needs whose Allium rules or guarantees its @allium-… tags cover (in plain Gherkin, the Feature it sits under). A test run claims it with an Allure tag label of the same id. Avoid: design input, DI-n, spec item, story, ticket, the test, sub-criterion

Stamp: The id tag a scenario carries: never renumbered, never reused, kept when the scenario is reworded. Whoever owns the spec stamps it (a factory's stamper, or a person); a scenario without one blocks a release. RDM never stamps. Avoid: id assignment, numbering

Baseline acceptance criterion: A requirement that no risk's controls name. Avoid: functional requirement, happy path

Risk-based acceptance criterion: A requirement a risk's controls name. It counts as met only when it is verified and the residual risk of the risk it controls is acceptable. Avoid: safety requirement, mitigation requirement

Bounded context: A unit of design: one context of the spec, one slice of its plan. It is drawn where the language changes, not where the workflow does, and named for its domain, never for what its code does or the technology it uses. Avoid: module, component, service, container, stage, layer

Task acceptance criterion: A checklist item on a planning task. Planning, never the record: it is not a requirement and nothing verifies it. Avoid: acceptance criterion (unqualified), requirement

docs.title: The record and its gates
docs.text:
Design record: Everything RDM audits, in git: the spec, the design documents, the risk register, the validation records, the controlled documents and the tests. It is the only source of truth; the spec changes in the factory's own process, the rest only by a reviewed pull request. Avoid: database, docs

Design history file: The design record as a regulator receives it: the documents rendered from the record, with their evidence. Abbreviated DHF. The dhf/ directory rdm adopt and rdm init lay down holds the record those documents are rendered from; it is named for what it becomes. Avoid: the record (for the rendered output)

Frontmatter: The YAML block between --- lines at the top of a Markdown document: its id, revision and title, and the record's declarations (risks, the risk policy, the contexts and references of a document). The gates read them from it. Avoid: header, metadata block

Design document: The controlled document of one bounded context that describes how the context meets the requirements of its slice of the spec. Avoid: spec, SDD (unqualified)

Design output: The architecture that meets a bounded context's requirements: its components, what each is responsible for, and how they relate, in its design document. It names components, never source files or functions. Avoid: implementation notes, module list, code walkthrough

Controlled document: A document with an id and a revision whose every change goes through review. Avoid: doc, file

Approved: Said of a design document that is committed and merged through a reviewed pull request. Git is the approval record; no sign-off table repeats it. Avoid: signed off, accepted

Independent review: Approval of a pull request by someone other than its author: the record's independent verification. An agent never gives it. Avoid: code review (unqualified), self-review

Code coverage: How much of a unit's code its unit tests run: a unit-test measure. Never acceptance evidence, never carried in Allure, never in the record's traceability; RDM does not read it. Not checklist coverage (the clauses the documents reference). Avoid: coverage (unqualified), test coverage (for the requirements a test verifies)

Release gate: The check that blocks a release until the spec is read whole (every scenario stamped, no id twice), it holds at least one requirement, every requirement is verified, every user need is addressed by a requirement covering its rules or guarantees, and the risk rules raise no blocking finding. It warns, never blocks, on a user need with no approved validation record. Whether the runs are release-grade evidence is shown by the verification report and the knowledge graph, not decided by the gate. Avoid: CI, green build

Design specification: The core bounded context: the spec, read — its user needs and requirements. It depends on no other context; every other context conforms to its ids. It reads a specification and never polices how one is written: that is the factory's (ADR 0002). Avoid: design controls (for this context; the term names the regulatory process RDM as a whole implements), requirements module

Release: The bounded context that decides whether a release may go ahead: the release gate over verified status, risk and validation. It reads the specification, test evidence and risk; none of them reads it. The evidence a release keeps is published by publishing. Avoid: deployment, CI (for the context)

Shared kernel: The helpers every bounded context may use and that use none: YAML and files, ids, git, frontmatter, the reconcile helpers. Not a context: it has no language of its own and owns no requirement. Avoid: utils, common, core (the core is the design specification)

Composition root: The one place that wires the command line to every context (rdm/main.py). It is in no context, so it may import any. Avoid: main module, glue

docs.title: Verification and validation
docs.text:
Test: An automated check tagged with the requirement it verifies. It verifies the acceptance criterion; it is not the criterion. Avoid: acceptance criterion, scenario, spec

Verification step: One named check within a test, with its own result; a test is the ordered set of its verification steps. It belongs to the test, never to the acceptance criterion: a failed step fails the test, and the requirement stays one criterion however many steps check it. Avoid: acceptance criterion, clause, sub-criterion, assertion

Test run: One execution of a test, at one commit, by one executor. Avoid: build, job, test case

Executor: Who or what ran a test run: a CI job or a person's machine, recorded with the run. Avoid: runner, agent (for the executor)

Test evidence: The bounded context that takes test results in the formats tools write them (Allure) and translates them into test runs of the record's tests, labelled with the commit under test. The tools' own words (result, label, container) stop at its boundary. Avoid: test results (for the context), reports

Verified: Said of a requirement with a passing run of a test tagged with it and no failed one. It shows the requirement is met, not that the test proves it. Avoid: validated, tested, done

Release-grade evidence: Verification in which every requirement is verified, no run failed, and every run tested the record's commit with no uncommitted changes. Avoid: green build, passing CI

Validated: Said of a user need whose intended users, in its intended use, were shown to reach its result. Avoid: verified, accepted

Traceability matrix: The table from user need to requirement to test to result, generated from the record and the test runs. It is never edited. Avoid: trace table, RTM (unqualified)

Evidence bundle: A release's verification data, traceability matrix and executed results with every attachment they reference, in one archive with a manifest. Avoid: artifact, report

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Compliance: The bounded context that holds standards as checklists and checks the controlled documents against them. Avoid: gap analysis (for the context; it is the activity), audit

Checklist: A selection of a standard's clauses that a set of documents must reference, composable by including other checklists. Avoid: standard (for the selection), template

Checklist clause: One requirement of a standard, as a checklist lists it, named by its key. A controlled document references it; nothing in a test does. Avoid: clause (unqualified), requirement, criterion

Gap: A checklist clause that no controlled document references. Coverage is the share of a checklist's clauses that are referenced. Avoid: finding, missing item (unqualified)

Checklist reference: A checklist clause's key written in a controlled document inside [[ … ]] ([[62304:5.1.1]]), saying where the document meets the clause. Only text inside the brackets counts; a bare mention does not. Avoid: tag (a tag names a requirement on a test), citation

docs.title: Risk
docs.text:
Risk analysis: Identifying the hazard, the sequence of events, the hazardous situation, the harm, and the estimate of its probability and severity. Avoid: risk assessment (for this step alone)

Risk evaluation: Comparing a risk estimate with the risk acceptability criteria, giving acceptable or unacceptable. Without approved criteria it is blocked, not guessed. Avoid: risk scoring, risk rating

Risk acceptability criteria: The project's own severities, probabilities, levels and the acceptability of each level, approved before any risk is evaluated against them. Not a universal matrix. Avoid: standard risk matrix, ISO matrix

Hazardous situation: A circumstance in which people, property or the environment are exposed to one or more hazards. Not the harm, and not the cause. Avoid: hazard, threat, scenario

Harm: The injury or damage that a hazardous situation can lead to. Defined once and referenced, so its severity cannot diverge between the risks that share it. Avoid: impact, consequence

Harm pathway: One pair of a hazardous situation and a harm, carrying its own probability. One situation can have several, each with its own severity and probability. Avoid: risk line, risk row

STRIDE threat: A security threat classified as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege. It complements safety analysis and may link to a safety risk; it does not replace it. Avoid: vulnerability, attack (for the classified threat)

Risk control: Something done to reduce a risk, allocated to a requirement that implements it. Defined once and referenced from every harm pathway it bears on. Avoid: measure, mitigation, safeguard

Control effect: What one risk control does to one harm pathway's probability, whether relative or absolute, and where it sits in the order controls are applied. Avoid: measure effect, reduction, impact

Effective: Said of a risk control that is verified and whose risk has been evaluated again with an acceptable residual. A passing test alone makes a control verified, not effective. The record shows both facts; judging that the control does what it is meant to stays a person's. Avoid: controlled, mitigated, done

Initial risk / residual risk: The same assessment at two stages: before any risk control, and after the applied controls fold together. Stages are rows, not a before-and-after pair of columns. Avoid: gross risk, net risk, pre/post mitigation

Proposal: A rating, a control, an acceptability criterion or a verification plan that no person has approved yet. It is shown as a proposal until someone approves it. Avoid: draft, assumption, default

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Publishing: The bounded context that renders the design record into controlled documents: templates filled with data generated from the record, then Markdown, PDF and DOCX. It reads the record; it never changes it. Avoid: rendering (for the context), export

Template: A controlled document's source, with placeholders that generated data fills. The rendered document is output, not source. Avoid: form, the document (for the source)

Data file: A YAML file whose content a template renders, named in the template by the file's name without its extension (data/device.yml is device). Avoid: config (a render configuration names the extensions, not data)

Audit note: Any [[ … ]] text in a template, checklist references among them: kept in the auditor's copy of a rendered document, removed from the engineers' copy by the audit-note extension. Avoid: comment, annotation

Reference document: A Word file whose styles, header and footer Pandoc gives every rendered Word document. Avoid: Word template (it is not a template of the record)

Device master record index: The generated list of controlled documents (id, title, path, revision) a DMR document renders. Abbreviated DMR index. Avoid: document list, register (the risk register is another thing)

Instructions for use (IFU): The product's instructions for anyone who uses it; in plain words, its user manual (RDM's is its documentation site). A design output, listed page by page by a controlled document of kind manual, so the DMR index holds it. What it must teach is stated as requirements. Avoid: docs (unqualified), help

docs.title: Knowledge graph
docs.text:
Knowledge graph: The record — the spec, its test runs, history, risks and checklists — projected into RDF with RDM's vocabulary, for people and agents to query. Read-only and rebuilt from the record: never edited, never the source of a fact. graph names it in commands and code. Avoid: database, knowledge base, graph model, the record (for the graph)

Projection: Turning one source of the record into facts of the knowledge graph, one named graph per source. Avoid: import, sync, export

Vocabulary: The classes and properties the knowledge graph uses: the published language that queries and agents rely on. Avoid: schema (for the vocabulary), data model

Gate rule: A shape over the knowledge graph. A violation blocks a release; a warning only informs the reviewer. Avoid: lint, constraint (unqualified)

docs.title: Worked example: Löyly's pi harness
docs.text:
examples/loyly-pi-harness keeps the design history file of a real product with RDM, from outside it: the regeneration harness of Löyly, an agentic software factory. Its spec (spec v2) holds 201 requirements as stamped Gherkin scenarios in six contexts, with user needs in an event model, Allium rules and an event storm; six clojure.test suites verify it. Löyly knows nothing of RDM or Allure:

  • RDM reads the spec from its loyly submodule (spec: in the example's dhf/config.yml), its needs through the Löyly adapter.
  • run-acceptance.sh runs the harness's suites unchanged, with a small bridge (bridge/user.clj) on the JVM's boot class path that writes each test as an Allure result, tagged with the requirement it claims and labelled with the Löyly commit it tested.
  • The harness is a tool, so it is validated as one, with computer software validation (after FDA's Computer Software Assurance guidance and ISO 13485 4.1.6), not as a medical device. The whole validation is one document (dhf/documents/tool_validation.md): intended use, the process risk with ten risks (four of them about its AI agents, the builder and the grading agent) that the release gate evaluates, the assurance, the record, Part 11 for the system that keeps it, and change; it is checked against the built-in csv_tool_validation and part11_document_control checklists.
  • RDM's gates then hold the harness to its own spec: all 201 requirements verified, every need addressed, every risk evaluated, every CSV and Part 11 clause referenced; the evidence bundle carries the verification report. CI runs it all on every change to RDM.

Its README says how to run it. Its traceability, from its knowledge graph, the same way as RDM's own (from the spec alone when the build has no results of its suites):

tests run at Find Fit allFit selectionFull screen

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Every change goes round the same loop. Start with Changing the record; the other guides go deeper on one part of it.

 the Gherkin spec ───► tag the tests ──► run the gates ──► review and merge
   (tagged scenarios)     (record)          (gates)            (your forge)
        ▲                                                       │
        └──────── query the graph, render the documents ◄───────┘
Task Page Make a change, step by step Changing the record Read the spec, write the tests that claim its requirements The spec and its tests Keep the risk register and its controls Risk register Record validation evidence Validation evidence Run the release gate The gates Check documents against a standard's checklist Gap analysis Run the gates in CI The gates in your CI Query the record as a graph The record as a graph Browse the graph Browsing in Graph Explorer Let agents read the record For agents Render documents Authoring and rendering

When a step fails, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: For agents
docs.text: An agent working on a regulated product needs the same answers a reviewer does — what does this requirement say, which test runs verify it, did they pass at this commit, which risks does it control — and it must not be able to change the answers. rdm graph mcp gives it the record as a read-only knowledge source: it reads the current spec, Markdown and test results on every call, and it has no way to write.

docs.title: Register the server
docs.text:
rdm graph mcp serves the record to an agent as a Model Context Protocol server over stdio, which most agent harnesses speak. Register it once; for Claude Code, in the project's .mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rdm": {
      "command": "rdm",
      "args": ["graph", "mcp", "--dhf", "dhf", "--allure-results", "dhf/allure-results"]
    }
  }
}

Other harnesses take the same command and arguments in their own MCP settings.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool Answers trace a requirement (by its id: its scenario, rule, context, source, user needs, runs with steps and attachments, the source files they exercise, risks controlled), a user need (by its id, a Feature's title: its text and requirements; with the Löyly adapter also its actors, surfaces, rules, guarantees and storm events), or a risk (its chain, scores and controlling requirements, risk register) query any read-only SPARQL (SELECT, ASK, CONSTRUCT, DESCRIBE), prefixes predeclared, capped at 200 rows by default with truncated saying when schema the vocabulary and prefixes, so the agent can write its own queries validate the gate shapes' results: violations and warnings

Every call projects the record afresh (a fraction of a second), so an agent editing a branch sees its own edits on the next call — there is no store to rebuild.

docs.title: Read-only by construction
docs.text: It cannot change anything or reach the network. There is no write tool, query refuses SERVICE (a federated query would make the server send HTTP requests), trace takes only an id, and query refuses SPARQL Update. An agent that wants to change the record does what a person does: changes the spec where it is kept, or edits the Markdown and tests and opens a pull request for review.

docs.title: Changing the record
docs.text:
Every change that alters what the product does reaches the record the same way. The spec changes in its own process (a scenario written and tagged with an id, by the team or by the factory that owns the spec); the tests, documents and risks change in one pull request, reviewed by someone other than its author. That review is the approval; the merge records it.

 WHO needs it              WHAT it must do                PROOF it does it
 User need: a Feature ◄──── Requirement  @REQ-12  ◄────────── Acceptance test
                     under  (tagged scenario)        claims  @allure.tag("REQ-12")
                                                                   │ executed
 Traceability matrix ◄─────── verification.yml ◄────────────── Allure results

docs.title: Do I need a requirement?
docs.text:
• The change alters behaviour, an interface or an output: it is governed by a requirement. If one covers it (ask the graph: trace REQ-12 in rdm graph mcp, or a rdm graph query), keep its test passing; if none does, the spec needs a new scenario.
  • A refactor, documentation, comments or CI plumbing: no spec work. The gates still run and should stay green.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. The spec. The scenario is written under the Feature (the user need) it serves and tagged with a new id: The spec and its tests.
  2. The test. Write the acceptance test that verifies it, tagged @allure.tag("REQ-12") (a Gherkin runner writes the tag for you), and the code that makes it pass.
  3. Risks. If the requirement controls a risk, name it in the risk's controls: (Risk register).

  4. The gates. Run the acceptance suite and the gates as CI does:

    pytest tests/acceptance --clean-alluredir --alluredir=dhf/allure-results
rdm story verify --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results -o dhf/data/verification.yml
rdm story release-gate --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results

  5. The review. Open the pull request. The reviewer reads each changed scenario beside its test and judges whether the test proves it.

Planning artifacts (tasks, issues, boards) coordinate the work; they are never evidence (Plan vs. record).

docs.title: RDM's gates in your CI
docs.text:
Any repository can run RDM's gates in GitHub Actions without copying them. RDM publishes three pieces. Each one installs RDM from the revision you pin, never by name from a package index. (PyPI's rdm is another project.)

Piece Use it for Pinned as Reusable workflow .github/workflows/gates.yml the whole job: your acceptance tests, then verify, the release gate, graph validation and the evidence bundle scope-impact/rdm/.github/workflows/gates.yml@<ref> Composite action actions/gates the gates as steps in a workflow of your own, after your tests scope-impact/rdm/actions/gates@<ref> Composite action at the root rendering the documents to PDF, in the RDM image of the same release scope-impact/rdm@<ref>

rdm adopt lays down a workflow that calls the reusable workflow, pinned to the RDM release that ran the adoption. RDM's own CI calls the same workflow, pinned to the commit under test, so the workflow you call is the one RDM gates itself with.

docs.title: The reusable workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/design-controls.yml
name: Design controls
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  design-controls:
    uses: scope-impact/rdm/.github/workflows/gates.yml@main
    with:
      rdm-ref: main                     # the same ref as after the @
      install-command: pip install -e .   # your own dependencies, if the tests need them

A reusable workflow cannot see the ref it was called at, so you write the ref twice: after the @, and as rdm-ref. The workflow checks out RDM at rdm-ref and installs RDM, pytest and allure-pytest from that checkout. To upgrade, change both refs together.

A tag can be moved; a commit sha cannot. For the strictest pin, use the release's commit sha in both places, with the tag as a comment: gates.yml@<sha> # <tag>. Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem keeps both the sha and the comment current. RDM pins its own third-party actions that way. The workflow asks only for contents: read. Inputs reach its scripts through environment variables, never spliced into the script text.

Input Default rdm-ref — (required) the RDM tag or sha the workflow is pinned to rdm-repository scope-impact/rdm a fork, say python-version 3.12 dhf dhf the design history file install-rdm true installs RDM, pytest and allure-pytest from rdm-ref; false when install-command already does install-command none installs your dependencies before the tests submodules false true (or recursive) checks out your submodules, for a spec kept in one acceptance-tests true false until you have a tagged acceptance test test-command pytest tests/acceptance --clean-alluredir --alluredir=dhf/allure-results allure-results dhf/allure-results where test-command writes its results release-gate true false until your first requirement's test lands graph-validate true the gate rules as SHACL, plus graph-only warnings checklists none space-separated checklists for graph validation (rdm gap --list) evidence-bundle true writes the release evidence bundle, including the verification report PDF, and uploads it as rdm-evidence allure-report true renders the Allure HTML report and uploads it as allure-report

The verification record (the Allure results and verification.yml) is uploaded as verification-record, even when a gate fails.

A required status check on the caller's side is named after both jobs: design-controls / gates.

docs.title: Phased adoption
docs.text: A freshly adopted repository may have no spec and no tagged tests yet. The workflow rdm adopt lays down sets acceptance-tests: false and release-gate: false, so the release gate waits. Set both to true when the spec is in place and your first tagged test lands. If the spec is a submodule, set submodules: 'true' (or submodules: true on the checkout in a workflow of your own) and name its plan directory as spec: in dhf/config.yml.

docs.title: The gates action, in a workflow of your own
docs.text:
When your tests need their own setup (services, a build matrix, another language), run them your way, then add the gates as a step:

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      # ... your own setup and tests, writing Allure results to dhf/allure-results
      - uses: scope-impact/rdm/actions/gates@main
        with:
          checklists: 62304_2015_class_b

The action installs RDM with the graph extra from its own revision, then runs the same steps the reusable workflow does. It takes the workflow's gate inputs (dhf, allure-results, release-gate, graph-validate, checklists, evidence-bundle), plus artifact-name, python-version, and install-rdm (false when RDM is already installed from the same revision). Verify and the evidence bundle run only when there are Allure results.

docs.title: Rendering the documents
docs.text:
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: scope-impact/rdm@main

The action runs make pdfs in ghcr.io/scope-impact/rdm and uploads the PDFs. The image tag follows the action's ref: @vX.Y.Z renders with image X.Y.Z and @v1 with image 1. A branch or a sha falls back to latest. Set version to choose the image yourself.

docs.title: Authoring and rendering documents
docs.text:
RDM's core pipeline turns YAML data + Jinja2 Markdown templates into regulatory documents:

data/*.yml  +  documents/*.md (Jinja2)  →  rdm render  →  Markdown  →  Pandoc/Typst → PDF/DOCX

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
rdm render <template.md> <config.yml> [data files…] > output.md

The template path is relative to the working directory (run it from the project root, as the Makefile does). A value the template uses but no data file gives, or a template that does not exist, is an error naming it.

  • config.yml configures rendering: the Markdown extensions to run over the rendered document (below). An empty file loads none.
  • Each data file becomes a template variable named after its file stem: data/history.yml is {{ history }} in the template, so a top-level entries: list in that file is history.entries.
---
id: SOP-001
revision: 2
title: "My controlled document"
---

# Revision history
{% for entry in history.entries %}
| {{ entry.revision }} | {{ entry.date }} | {{ entry.change }} |
{%- endfor %}

docs.title: Markdown extensions, and the auditor's and engineer's copies
docs.text:
md_extensions in config.yml lists the extensions, run in order over the rendered lines; code is never touched:

Extension What it does rdm.md_extensions.SectionNumberExtension numbers the headings (# 1, ## 1.1) rdm.md_extensions.VocabularyExtension gives the template the words the document uses, for a glossary or acronym list of only those terms rdm.md_extensions.AuditNoteExclusionExtension removes every [[…]] note, the checklist references among them

The [[62304:5.1.1]] references are what gap analysis reads, so keep them in the source. They show in the rendered document unless the audit-note extension removes them: render the auditor's copy without it (the references show where each clause is met) and the engineers' copy with it, from two configuration files.

docs.title: Template helpers
docs.text: Helper What it does invert_dependencies group items by the things they depend on (e.g. tests per requirement) join_to join foreign keys to rows in another table by id; an id the table lacks is an error naming it, never a blank row md_indent indent an included snippet, optionally shifting its heading levels first_pass_output two-pass rendering: reference content computed later in the document (e.g. a table of contents over generated sections)

docs.title: Collecting snippets from source
docs.text:
Keep fragments of documentation next to the code and pull them into documents:

rdm collect src/**/*.py > data/snippets.yml

Delimit snippets in any text file with RDOC <name> … ENDRDOC; each becomes a named entry you can render with {{ snippets.<name> }}. A name used twice, in one file or in two, is refused, naming where, and rdm collect exits 2.

docs.title: Test results in documents
docs.text: Verification evidence comes from Allure results through rdm story verify: that path feeds the gates and the traceability matrix, which a document renders.

docs.title: Frontmatter conventions for controlled documents
docs.text:
Every controlled document declares its identity in YAML frontmatter:

---
id: SOP-001        # stable identity
revision: 2        # bumped per approved change
title: "…"
---

Requirements and user needs are not in frontmatter: they are the spec RDM reads (The spec and its tests).

docs.title: PDF and Word
docs.text:
A project from rdm init builds its documents with make: make renders release/*.md, make pdfs the PDFs (Pandoc to Typst, styled by template.typ) and make docs Word files. In CI, the PDF action runs make pdfs in the RDM image.

Pandoc's table model has no column or row spans and no vertical rules; raw Typst in the Markdown is the way out when a table needs them.

The PDF's look is template.typ's: the palette at its top (maroon for headings and the cover, charcoal, ivory, nexus), body-font and mono-font, and the cover. To brand it, change those; to add a logo, place the image in the project and add image("logo.svg", width: 3cm) to the cover block. The cover and header read the document's frontmatter: id, revision, title, date (the build date when absent) and status ("Draft" when absent). The fonts must be installed where the PDF is built: Nunito Sans and JetBrains Mono, with Noto Sans and DejaVu Sans Mono standing in; the Docker setup has them.

For Word, give Pandoc your company template as a reference document: start from Pandoc's own, pandoc -o reference.docx --print-default-data-file reference.docx, style it, and add reference-doc: reference.docx to pandoc_docx.yml. The output takes its styles, header and footer, and make rebuilds the Word files when it changes. Pandoc writes each frontmatter key as a Word document property, so the header can show the document's id, revision and title: in the reference document choose Insert → Field, pick DocProperty, and then the property (Pandoc's are lower case, at the bottom of the list).

docs.title: Gap analysis — check documents against a standard
docs.text:
rdm gap checks that your documents reference every clause a standard's checklist lists. A reference is a [[KEY]] block in a document, such as [[62304:5.1.1]] or [[This section fulfills X-1 and X-2]]; the checklist maps keys to the standard's clauses. Only text inside [[ … ]] counts, and a dotted descendant covers its parent. The exact reading and matching rules are the compliance design.

rdm gap --list                                          # the built-in checklists
rdm gap 62304_2015_class_b documents/*.md               # exit 0 = covered; 3 = gaps, listed
rdm gap --coverage 62304_2015_class_b FDA-SW_2021_basic documents/*.md   # one row per checklist
rdm gap --coverage -v 62304_2015_class_b documents/*.md # …and name the missing clauses

Both exit 3 when a clause is missing, and 2 when nothing could be checked: a checklist with no clauses, or a checklist, include or document that cannot be read. A document that still holds a TODO placeholder is named in a warning: a fresh rdm init project references every clause from templates that say nothing yet, so its coverage means nothing until they are written.

The built-ins cover IEC 62304, ISO 14971, the FDA software, cybersecurity and human-factors guidances, part11_document_control: the 21 CFR Part 11 controls for document control in git, and csv_tool_validation: computer software validation of a tool used in production or the quality system (after FDA's Computer Software Assurance guidance and ISO 13485 4.1.6 and 7.5.6). Each item of these two names its source PDF, section and page. Audit your own document-control procedure and tool validation against them:

rdm gap part11_document_control dhf/documents/document_control.md
rdm gap csv_tool_validation dhf/documents/tool_validation.md

RDM holds its own document control and its own tool validation to them, and so does the worked example, for Löyly's pi harness.

docs.title: Your own checklists
docs.text:
A checklist is a plain text file. Each line is a clause key followed by its description; # starts a comment; include <name> pulls in a built-in checklist by name or another file, relative to the including one:

include 62304_2015_class_b
QMS-1 our additional internal requirement

There is no way to exclude a clause. Either reference it from a document that says where it is met or why it does not apply, or start from a copy: the gap report prints the missing clauses in checklist format, so rdm gap 62304_2015_class_b > my_checklist.txt gives you a checklist to edit.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
Run gap analysis as a required check, so a document set cannot merge with a clause no document references:

- run: rdm gap 62304_2015_class_b dhf/documents/*.md

docs.title: The gates
docs.text:
The gates decide pass or block from the record; they never change it. Each runs the same way locally and in CI. In the CI workflow rdm adopt installs, the acceptance tests and release gate are inputs set to false until your first requirement's test lands (phased adoption).

Gate Blocks Runs Release gate — rdm story release-gate a release unless the spec is read whole, every requirement is verified by a passing tagged run, every user need is addressed, and every risk is evaluated, its risk controls verified and its residual acceptable CI Gap analysis — rdm gap documents that do not reference every clause a checklist requires on demand; add it to CI Graph validation — rdm graph validate the same rules, as SHACL shapes over the graph (what the release gate blocks about the whole record, such as an unreadable document or result, is on the record's node), plus warnings the coded gates do not give on demand; add it to CI

The rules each gate applies, and what it reports, are its design: release gate, risk rules, gap analysis, graph shapes.

docs.title: Release gate
docs.text:
pytest tests/acceptance --clean-alluredir --alluredir=dhf/allure-results
rdm story verify --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results -o dhf/data/verification.yml
rdm story release-gate --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results

It blocks, each one named, on:

Event When No Spec no feature files were found (spec/ or features/ at the repository root, or a .pi/plan), and dhf/config.yml names no spec: Unstamped Scenario a scenario carries no id tag Item Stamped Twice one id is on more than one scenario Unreadable Spec a file of the spec cannot be read (with the Löyly adapter: an event-model or event-storm file) No Requirements the spec holds no tagged scenario: nothing to verify Requirement Failed / Requirement Untested a run claiming the requirement failed or broke; or no run claiming it passed Unreadable Result a result file it cannot read: it could hold a failed run Need Unaddressed a user need no requirement addresses (a Feature with no tagged scenario; with the Löyly adapter, a need none of whose rules or guarantees a scenario covers) Risk Finding a blocking finding of the risk rules

It warns, never blocks, on a user need without an approved human validation record (a machine cannot supply that judgment, but its absence is never silent), on a proposed risk, and on a tag that looks like an id but names no requirement.

docs.title: Gap analysis
docs.text:
rdm gap 62304_2015_class_b dhf/documents/*.md

See gap analysis.

docs.title: Graph validation
docs.text:
rdm graph validate --allure-results dhf/allure-results --checklist part11_document_control

The gate rules as SHACL shapes (rdm/graph/shapes.ttl). An acceptance test holds them to blocking exactly what the release gate and rdm gap block; the coded gates stay authoritative. It exits 1 on any violation.

Violations, which block:

Rule Why a user need no requirement addresses an unaddressed need a requirement with no passing test run, or with a failed or broken one unverified a checklist clause no document references a gap against the standard a clause without a key or a standard; a checklist member that is not a clause malformed checklist data a requirement id on more than one scenario one id, one scenario a risk with no id, hazard, situation, harm or category; a security risk with no STRIDE category; a risk id declared twice an incomplete register a risk not evaluated against a risk policy; a recorded level the policy contradicts; controls with no residual score; a control or link naming nothing declared; an unknown status; a residual that does not allow release the risk rules (risk register) a document referencing a document the record does not hold a dangling reference

Warnings, reported, never blocking:

Rule Why a requirement that addresses no user need the spec does not say whom it serves a test run claiming an item id that is no requirement of the spec a claim that resolves to nothing a test run tied to no commit the version it is evidence for is unknown a test run of another commit than the product's stale evidence a document whose latest change has not landed on the default branch not yet merged a risk with status: proposed no person has approved its rating

Add your own rules as more shape files, with no code change:

rdm graph validate --shapes team-rules.ttl

@prefix sh:  <http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#> .
@prefix rdm: <https://github.com/scope-impact/rdm/ns#> .
@prefix dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> .

[] a sh:NodeShape ;
   sh:targetClass rdm:Document ;
   sh:property [ sh:path dcterms:title ; sh:minCount 1 ;
                 sh:message "every controlled document needs a title" ] .

docs.title: Independent review
docs.text: A passing test proves code ran, not that the requirement is met. That judgment belongs to the pull-request reviewer, who must not be the change's author (the review step). The reviewer reads each changed test against its scenario's text and asks whether the test would fail if the code did not do what the scenario says.

docs.title: Release evidence
docs.text:
rdm story evidence-bundle --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results -o release-evidence/
rdm story evidence-report --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results -o verification_report.pdf
rdm story dmr documents/ -o data/dmr.yml

The evidence bundle is the retained release evidence: the verification data, the rendered traceability matrix, the executed Allure results with every attachment, the verification report and a manifest, ready to attach to a release tag so the evidence outlives CI retention.

The verification report shows what was run to verify each requirement, for someone who did not run it: an auditor, a notified body, the reviewer. It says whether the evidence is release-grade and why not, and ends with every result file's SHA-256 so it can be checked against the bundle. What it holds is item-07-009 in the publishing design. It needs Typst: install rdm[report], or have typst on PATH as the RDM image does. The reusable gates upload it in rdm-evidence.

dmr writes the device-master-record index (id, title, path and revision of each controlled document) from the documents' own frontmatter.

The user manual belongs in that index too: a controlled document of kind: manual lists its pages under pages: (paths from the project root), and the pages stay where the site builds them. RDM's own manual is dhf/documents/user_manual.md.

docs.title: Browsing in Graph Explorer
docs.text:
AWS Graph Explorer draws the graph and lets you search and expand it. It only reads: the endpoint it connects to refuses updates. Start the endpoint first:

rdm graph build --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results \
  --checklist part11_document_control --store .rdm/graph
rdm graph serve --store .rdm/graph

docs.title: Start Graph Explorer
docs.text:
With rdm graph serve running, start Graph Explorer and point it at the endpoint. On Linux, --network host lets the container reach localhost:7878:

docker run --rm --network host \
  --env HOST=localhost \
  --env PROXY_SERVER_HTTPS_CONNECTION=false \
  --env GRAPH_TYPE=sparql \
  --env USING_PROXY_SERVER=true \
  --env PUBLIC_OR_PROXY_ENDPOINT=http://localhost \
  --env GRAPH_CONNECTION_URL=http://localhost:7878 \
  public.ecr.aws/neptune/graph-explorer

Open http://localhost/explorer, search for a requirement (for example item-04-001), add it, and expand its neighbors: its user need, its context and the test runs that claim it appear as edges.

On macOS or Windows (Docker Desktop), drop --network host, add -p 80:80, and use GRAPH_CONNECTION_URL=http://host.docker.internal:7878. Newer Graph Explorer releases need only GRAPH_CONNECTION_URL (the USING_PROXY_SERVER / PUBLIC_OR_PROXY_ENDPOINT pair is the older form, still honored). A 404 for /rdf/statistics/summary in the browser console is harmless: that summary is a Neptune-only endpoint, and Graph Explorer falls back without it.

docs.title: Make it readable
docs.text:
Graph Explorer keeps these settings in the browser, so you set them once:

  • Namespaces → Custom: add rdm = https://github.com/scope-impact/rdm/ns#. Classes and edges then read rdm:Clause, rdm:includes instead of an auto-generated prefix.
  • Styles → Resources → Customize each type: set Display Name to rdfs:label, so nodes show item-04-001, P11:11.10a, 62304_2015_class_c rather than IRIs. Every node in the graph carries a label. A different shape per type helps too (for example a star for standards and a tag for documents).
  • Search finds nodes by rdfs:label; the Class filter set to skos:ConceptScheme with Add All puts every loaded standard on the canvas at once.
  • Expand (sidebar) expands the selected node, optionally to one neighbor type, for example only rdm:Checklist to follow an include chain. Expansion is capped at 10 neighbors by default (Settings).

Graph Explorer v3.2.2's Search → Query panel runs a SELECT against the endpoint and lists the rows (paste the query, Submit) — for example every risk with its controls, their verifying tests and runs. It cannot draw those rows, and it asks for CONSTRUCT results as JSON, which a standard SPARQL endpoint rejects: build pictures from search and expansion or a graph file (below), and use rdm graph query for scripted questions (the record as a graph).

docs.title: The whole record at once
docs.text:
Write a Graph Explorer graph file and load it with Load graph from file (the folder icon in the Graph View toolbar), with rdm graph serve running:

rdm graph explorer-file --store .rdm/graph -o rdm.graph.json
# a calmer picture: leave out test runs, commits and authors
rdm graph explorer-file --store .rdm/graph -o rdm-core.graph.json \
  --exclude TestRun --exclude Activity --exclude Agent

The file lists every node and every link between nodes; Graph Explorer fetches labels and properties from the endpoint (--endpoint, default http://localhost:7878). --exclude also leaves out what hangs only from the excluded nodes — without test runs, their steps, attachments and parameters go too, so the core view holds the record and nothing that floats. Expect a cluster per bounded context — its design inputs, their needs, documents and tests — and one per checklist.

docs.title: The record as a graph
docs.text:
rdm graph projects the record into RDF — the spec (user needs, requirements, bounded contexts), controlled documents, test results, git commits, the risk register, and the regulatory checklists your documents are held to — so you can query it with SPARQL, check it against the gate rules as SHACL shapes, browse it visually in AWS Graph Explorer, and let agents read it through a read-only MCP server.

The record stays the only thing anyone edits. The graph is derived: it is rebuilt from the record on every run, and Graph Explorer only browses it. To change something, change the spec or the Markdown and rebuild.

Page For this page building, querying and serving the graph, and what is in it The gates rdm graph validate: the gate rules as shapes, and adding your own Browsing in Graph Explorer seeing the record as a picture For agents the read-only MCP server

It needs the graph extra (installation). What the graph holds and why is its design: the knowledge graph.

docs.title: Build, query, serve
docs.text:
# Project the record (add --allure-results to include test runs,
# --checklist to include the checklists your documents are held to)
rdm graph build --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results \
  --checklist part11_document_control --store .rdm/graph
rdm graph build --dhf dhf -o dhf.nq          # or: sorted N-Quads, diffable

# Ask questions (rdm:, rdf:, rdfs:, xsd:, dcterms:, prov:, oslc_rm: are predeclared)
rdm graph query --store .rdm/graph \
  'SELECT ?id ?text WHERE { ?r a rdm:Requirement ; dcterms:identifier ?id ; rdm:text ?text } ORDER BY ?id'

# Serve it, read-only, as a SPARQL 1.1 endpoint at http://localhost:7878/sparql
rdm graph serve --store .rdm/graph            # localhost only; never bind a public address

--store is an embedded Oxigraph database. Each build clears it first, so a removed requirement never lingers. Without --store, rdm graph query builds an in-memory projection on the fly. Add .rdm/ to .gitignore; the store is generated, like Allure results. A built store, and the endpoint serving it, is as current as its last build; the agent server (rdm graph mcp) projects the record afresh on every call.

The endpoint is read-only. It allows requests from any origin so Graph Explorer can reach it, which is exactly why it accepts no update and no SERVICE call: any web page you have open could otherwise clear or forge the graph you are reviewing, or have it fetch addresses on your network. Every query is over the union of the named graphs, so FROM is refused rather than silently ignored: name a graph with GRAPH <…> { … }.

docs.title: The whole chain in one query
docs.text:
Run the acceptance suite, then project everything the record knows: needs, requirements, rules, contexts, documents, test runs, commits, and the checklists your documents are held to.

pytest tests/acceptance --clean-alluredir --alluredir=dhf/allure-results
rdm graph build --allure-results dhf/allure-results \
  --checklist part11_document_control --store .rdm/graph

The whole chain — need → requirement → context → test runs → results — is one query:

SELECT ?need ?requirement ?context
       (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?test; separator=" ") AS ?tests)
       (GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT ?status; separator="/") AS ?results)
WHERE {
  ?r a rdm:Requirement ; dcterms:identifier ?requirement ; rdm:ownedBy/rdfs:label ?context .
  OPTIONAL { ?r rdm:tracesTo/rdfs:label ?need }
  OPTIONAL { ?run rdm:exercises ?r ; rdfs:label ?test ; rdm:status ?status }
}
GROUP BY ?need ?requirement ?context
ORDER BY ?need ?requirement

docs.title: What is in the graph
docs.text:
One named graph per source, so a query can always tell where a fact came from. The endpoint's default graph is the union of all of them.

Graph Holds urn:dhf:<project>:graph/record the spec — user needs, requirements, bounded contexts (and, with the Löyly adapter, Allium rules) — and the controlled documents …graph/executions Allure results (only with --allure-results): each run's status, times, failure message and trace, parameters, steps and attachments, the requirements it claims and the source files it exercises …graph/git each controlled document's latest commit and its author, the commit that landed it on the default branch (rdm:landedIn, rdm:landedBy), and the commit the record was built at …graph/risks the risk register: each risk's chain, scores, computed levels, controls (rdm:controlledBy) and acceptance …graph/checklists the requested checklists: standards, clauses, checklists (--checklist) …graph/references documents' checklist references ([[KEY]]), linked to the clauses they name …graph/ontology RDM's vocabulary, so browsers can label classes and properties

Instances are named urn:dhf:<project>:<kind>/<id>, for example urn:dhf:rdm:requirement/item-04-001. <project> defaults to the repository name, so graphs from several repositories can be loaded into one store without collisions (--project overrides it).

The vocabulary (rdm/graph/ontology.ttl) reuses standards where they exist:

Term Meaning rdm:Requirement a tagged scenario of the spec, identified by its id tag; a subclass of oslc_rm:Requirement (OSLC Requirements Management); rdm:text its title, rdm:inRule its Gherkin Rule, rdm:source its file and line rdm:UserNeed a user need: a Feature, its description rdm:text rdm:BoundedContext, rdm:Document the other record entities Löyly adapter only rdm:covers and rdm:coversRule (the Allium obligations a requirement's tags name), rdm:AlliumRule with rdm:trigger, and on a need rdm:facing, rdm:surface, rdm:providesRule, rdm:guarantee, rdm:command, rdm:stormEvent rdm:tracesTo, rdm:ownedBy a requirement's needs, and the context of a requirement, need or rule rdm:TestRun rdm:exercises, rdm:testedAt, rdm:status results: a run, the requirements it claims, at a commit dcterms:identifier, dcterms:title, rdm:revision document metadata (Dublin Core) prov:wasGeneratedBy, prov:Activity, prov:Agent, prov:endedAtTime commits and authors (PROV-O) rdm:Clause ⊂ skos:Concept, rdm:Checklist ⊂ skos:Collection, skos:ConceptScheme clauses, checklists, standards (SKOS) dcterms:references a document claims a clause with a checklist reference ([[KEY]]), or names a document it relies on rdm:Risk, rdm:controlledBy, rdm:evaluatedAgainst the risk register (risk register) rdm:landedIn, rdm:landedBy, rdm:atCommit the commit that landed a document's change; the commit the record was built at

docs.title: Test results, in full
docs.text:
--allure-results brings in what each run says as evidence, not just pass or fail — and leaves out what the record already holds or what says nothing about design controls:

In Allure In the graph a result file an rdm:TestRun (a prov:Activity) with dcterms:identifier (uuid), rdm:fullName, rdm:status, prov:startedAtTime / prov:endedAtTime statusDetails rdm:statusMessage, rdm:statusTrace an id-shaped tag label rdm:exercises the requirement a commit label (rdm.pytest_plugin, item-03-002) rdm:testedAt that commit; worktree=dirty → rdm:uncommittedChanges (item-06-016) an output label (optional, a file path) rdm:exercisesOutput an rdm:SourceFile — the code the run exercises parameters rdm:parameter, each a name and a value steps, attachments rdm:step (nested, ordered), rdm:attachment (name, media type, file) other labels, links, historyId, containers not projected: they are the project's own or runner metadata, a test case is one-to-one with its run, and fixtures (tmp_path, capsys) say nothing about a requirement. The raw files stay in the evidence bundle.

So the chain runs all the way to code — requirement → run → source file — from labels the tests already carry, and trace lists a requirement's source files. Attachment content stays in the files (which the release bundle keeps); the graph holds the reference.

docs.title: Evidence tied to its version
docs.text: Each run links to the commit it tested, and rdm graph validate warns on stale evidence, a run tied to no commit, and a run claiming an id that is no requirement (item-06-016).

docs.title: Links between documents
docs.text:
For each controlled document the graph records the commit that landed its latest change on the default branch, and who landed it; git does not know who reviewed it (item-06-011). Two links come from frontmatter you write once (item-06-015):

# architecture.md — the bounded contexts, each with its part
contexts:
  - {id: specification, part: Record}
  - {id: release, part: Gates}
# any controlled document — the controlled documents it relies on
references: [DC-001]

Naming a document the record does not hold is a violation.

docs.title: Checklists are data
docs.text:
A standard, its clauses and the checklists that select them are instances, never classes, so a new standard is a new file and nothing else:

Concept In the graph Example Standard skos:ConceptScheme, named by the key prefix urn:rdm:standard:62304 Clause rdm:Clause with skos:notation (key), skos:definition, skos:inScheme, skos:broader (nearest listed dotted parent), rdm:edition urn:rdm:clause:62304:5.6.2 Checklist rdm:Checklist with skos:member (its own items) and rdm:includes (its includes) urn:rdm:checklist:62304_2015_class_b

A checklist's full contents are rdm:includes*/skos:member. Includes are kept as links, not flattened. Clause, standard and checklist IRIs carry no project name, so graphs from several repositories share one node per clause:

# Which documents, in which projects, claim each Part 11 clause?
SELECT ?key ?doc WHERE {
  <urn:rdm:checklist:part11_document_control> rdm:includes*/skos:member ?c .
  ?c skos:notation ?key .
  OPTIONAL { ?d dcterms:references ?c . BIND (STR(?d) AS ?doc) }
} ORDER BY ?key

To add a checklist, pass any of these to --checklist:

  • a built-in name (rdm gap --list);
  • a .txt file in rdm gap's checklist format;
  • an RDF file (.ttl, .nt, .jsonld, …) using the terms above, which is loaded as-is, so it can carry more than the text format, such as a standard's full title:
@prefix rdm:  <https://github.com/scope-impact/rdm/ns#> .
@prefix skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#> .

<urn:rdm:standard:IEC81001-5-1> a skos:ConceptScheme ;
    skos:prefLabel "IEC 81001-5-1:2021 Health software security" .
<urn:rdm:clause:IEC81001-5-1:5.1.1> a rdm:Clause ;
    skos:notation "IEC81001-5-1:5.1.1" ;
    skos:definition "secure software development process" ;
    skos:inScheme <urn:rdm:standard:IEC81001-5-1> .
<urn:rdm:checklist:security> a rdm:Checklist ;
    skos:member <urn:rdm:clause:IEC81001-5-1:5.1.1> .

References are matched with rdm gap's own key matcher: a descendant key covers its parent ([[62304:5.6.2.a]] covers 62304:5.6.2), a longer sibling never matches a shorter key, and only [[…]] blocks count. So a clause no document references in the graph is exactly an item rdm gap reports missing.

docs.title: Open world
docs.text:
The graph states only what the record states. A missing rdm:exercises edge means no run claimed it, not unverified; the absence of a fact is unknown, never false. Pass/fail judgments stay in the gates (rdm story release-gate). For example, this lists requirements no run claims:

SELECT ?id WHERE {
  ?r a rdm:Requirement ; dcterms:identifier ?id .
  FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?run rdm:exercises ?r }
}

docs.title: Risk register
docs.text:
The risk register is part of the record: risks are frontmatter in kind: risk documents under the DHF. The release gate holds the register to the rules a machine can check, and the graph carries it, so a query or an agent can walk risk → control → test → result.

The method — two branches from each user need (baseline acceptance criteria; safety and STRIDE risks), evaluating, controlling, verifying, re-evaluating — is the requirements and risk-analysis skills'. RDM keeps the register and checks it; it does not do the analysis.

docs.title: A risk
docs.text:
---
id: RMF-001
title: Risk register
kind: risk
risks:
  - id: RISK-DATA-001
    category: safety                 # safety or security
    hazard: "Lab report sync fails silently when the network drops."
    situation: "A user adds a report offline and assumes it synced."
    harm: "A health record is missing at a doctor's visit."
    severity: Serious                # from the harm
    probability: Possible            # from the situation, never the hazard
    controls: [REQ-4, REQ-7]             # each control is a requirement of the spec
    residual: {probability: Rare}    # add severity: where a control limits the harm itself
    acceptance:                      # only where the policy says justify for the residual level
      by: "Jane Doe (QA lead)"       # who accepted it
      rationale: "Further reduction is not practicable; sync failures are monitored weekly."
    status: approved                 # proposed until a person approves the rating
  - id: RISK-DATA-002
    category: security
    stride: Information disclosure   # Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure,
                                     # Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
    linked: [RISK-DATA-001]          # the safety risk this threat bears on, if any
    ...
---
  • A control is a requirement — a tagged scenario of the spec, named by its id. That gives the control a stated acceptance criterion, a tagged test and a result.
  • Levels are evaluated, not typed. RDM looks them up in your risk policy. You may also write level:; the gate checks it matches.
  • A residual is not evaluated until its controls are verified. Until every controlling requirement has a passing test, the residual decision is not evaluated and the release is blocked. A passing test shows the control was built as specified; whether it is effective is the reviewer's judgement.
  • status: proposed marks ratings no person has approved — an agent's suggestion, say. It is a warning at the release gate, never silent. A document-level status applies to every risk in it that sets none; with neither, the rating is proposed. The same holds for the policy: only status: approved is approved.

docs.title: The risk policy
docs.text:
There is no default. Acceptability criteria are yours, set before any individual risk decision — a matrix's cells are not ISO 14971 values. Declare one risk_policy in any DHF document's frontmatter (the risk management plan is the natural place); without it, a register with risks blocks the release as acceptability criteria missing. A second document declaring a risk_policy is refused, naming both, and so blocks as a malformed policy.

---
id: RMP-001
title: Risk acceptability policy
status: approved
risk_policy:
  severities: [Critical, Serious, Minor, Negligible]
  probabilities: [Rare, Unlikely, Possible, Likely]
  levels:                       # one level per probability, per severity
    Critical: [Medium, High, High, Block]
    Serious: [Low, Medium, High, High]
    Minor: [Low, Low, Medium, Medium]
    Negligible: [Low, Low, Low, Low]
  acceptability:                # per level: acceptable | justify | unacceptable
    Low: acceptable
    Medium: justify
    High: justify
    Block: unacceptable
---

The cells above are the risk-analysis skill's four-by-four, shown as a starting point; level names and cells are your choice. justify means acceptable only with an acceptance: naming by (who accepted it) and rationale (why further reduction is not reasonably practicable, and what monitors it).

docs.title: What the gates check, and what they do not
docs.text: The release gate blocks on a register it cannot evaluate or whose residuals the policy does not accept, and warns on proposed ratings; the rules are item-02-002 and item-02-003 in the risk design, and rdm graph validate reports the same through its shapes. Whether a control is effective, whether a residual is as low as reasonably practicable, and whether the analysis is honest are the reviewer's, using the skills.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
rdm graph query --allure-results dhf/allure-results 'SELECT ?risk ?decision ?control WHERE {
  ?r a rdm:Risk ; rdfs:label ?risk ; rdm:residualDecision ?decision .
  OPTIONAL { ?r rdm:controlledBy/rdfs:label ?control } } ORDER BY ?risk'

An agent connected to rdm graph mcp calls trace with a risk id, and gets the chain, the scores, the residual decision and each controlling requirement with its runs; the agent's trace of a requirement lists the risks it controls. From the command line, use the query above.

RDM's own policy and register, in its computer software validation, list the ways RDM itself could misreport evidence; an agent wrote them, so they are proposed until a maintainer approves them.

docs.title: The spec and its tests
docs.text: What RDM reads as your requirements, and how a test claims one. RDM does not author the spec: you, or a factory that writes and regenerates code from it (such as Löyly), keep it, written the Löyly way. RDM reads it, traces each requirement to the test runs that verify it, and gates the release on that. The words are the glossary's; what the gates then check is The gates.

docs.title: The model in one breath
docs.text: The spec is written the Löyly way. A requirement is an accepted Gherkin scenario, a concrete Given/When/Then example stamped with an id (@item-01-001). A user need is a screen of the event model, linked to the Allium surface that models it; a requirement addresses the needs whose Allium rules or guarantees its tags name. A test claims a requirement with an Allure tag label of the same id. Every entity and link is in the data model.

docs.title: Where the spec lives
docs.text:
rdm init and rdm adopt lay down a skeleton in .pi/ (adopt only when the repository has no spec yet); RDM finds it there without configuration:

.pi/
  plan/
    01-alarms -> ../spec/alarms        one slice per bounded context, in order
  spec/
    event-storm.edn                    the board: the domain's events and their causes
    alarms/
      spec.feature                     the accepted scenarios: the requirements
      drafts.feature                   scenarios not yet accepted (not read)
      allium/alarms.allium             rules, actors, surfaces and their guarantees
      event-model/area.edn             screens (the user needs), commands, events

The slice number NN is the first part of every id in that context (@item-01-SSS). A slice whose plan.md says status: planned or status: backlog is skipped and listed. Elsewhere, name the plan in dhf/config.yml (relative to the DHF): spec: ../.pi/plan.

docs.title: Requirements: stamped scenarios
docs.text:
Feature: Alarms
  The accepted scenarios of this context. Each is stamped with an item id
  that is never renumbered or reused.

  Rule: An alarm is raised within 2 s of a reading above the limit

    # alarms.allium, rule RaiseAlarm
    @allium-rule-success.RaiseAlarm
    @item-01-001
    Scenario: A reading above the limit raises an alarm within 2 s
      Given the limit for heart rate is 140
      When the monitor reads a heart rate of 150
      Then an alarm is raised within 2 s
  • The last id tag before a Scenario is its id, @item-NN-SSS by default. Other tags are kept, never read as ids.
  • RDM never assigns ids: a scenario with none is reported, and blocks the release, until whoever owns the spec stamps it. An id on two scenarios blocks too.
  • @allium-<kind>.<Name> names what the scenario covers: a rule's success or failure (rule-success.RaiseAlarm, rule-failure.RaiseAlarm.2) or a guarantee (guarantee.NeverSilenced). That is how it addresses a need.
  • The Rule: above a scenario, its title and its source line come along into the matrix and the graph.

docs.title: User needs: screens and surfaces
docs.text:
Each screen of a context's event model is a user need: its key the need's id (alarms/monitor), its description the need's text.

;; .pi/spec/alarms/event-model/area.edn
{:alarms
 {:screens
  {:alarms/monitor
   {:description "A nurse is alerted to a dangerous vital sign."
    :grain/allium [{:spec ".pi/spec/alarms/allium/alarms.allium" :kind :surface :name "Monitor"}]
    :commands #{:alarms/raise-alarm}}}}}

The surface it links says whom it faces, the rules it provides (by their triggers) and what it guarantees:

-- A nurse is alerted to a dangerous vital sign.
surface Monitor {
    facing nurse: Nurse
    provides:
        RaiseAlarm(monitor, reading)
    @guarantee NeverSilenced
        -- An alarm is never silenced without a nurse acknowledging it.
}

A requirement tagged with one of those rules or guarantees addresses the need; one tagged with none addresses its context's needs. The event-storm events the screen's commands produce, caused by an actor, show with the need. In a context with no screens, each surface is a need. The release gate blocks a need no requirement addresses. Validation is recorded against the need's id: validation evidence.

docs.title: Plain Gherkin
docs.text:
RDM's contract with a spec is only Gherkin and Allure (ADR 0002), so a spec kept as plain feature files works too: without .pi/plan, RDM looks for spec/**/*.feature, then features/**/*.feature; a requirement is any scenario with an id-shaped tag (@REQ-12), a user need each Feature (its description the need's text), and a context the directory a file sits in. Anywhere else, name it in dhf/config.yml:

spec:
  features: ["../acceptance/**/*.feature"]   # one or more globs
  exclude: ["**/drafts.feature"]             # optional
  id: "REQ-\\d+"                              # optional: the id tag's pattern, without "@"
  needs: feature                             # feature (the default), or allium

docs.title: Writing the test
docs.text:
A Gherkin runner (allure-pytest-bdd, allure-cucumber, allure-behave) writes each scenario's tags as Allure tag labels, so a run already claims its id. A plain test claims it with @allure.tag:

import allure

@allure.tag("item-01-001")                    # the link the whole chain hangs on
@allure.label("output", "src/alarms.py")     # optional: the code it exercises
def test_alarm_within_two_seconds(device):
    """item-01-001: an alarm within 2 s of a reading above the limit."""
    with allure.step("a reading above the limit raises an alarm"):
        alarm = device.read(150)
        allure.attach(repr(alarm), name="alarm")   # what the assertion looked at
        assert alarm.raised
    with allure.step("within 2 s"):
        assert alarm.latency_s <= 2
  • Check only what the scenario states, one verification step for each thing it requires, so a failure says what it was checking.
  • Attach what you checked, so the evidence shows more than "passed".
  • Only tag labels claim a requirement. A tag that names no requirement but looks like one (item_01_001) is warned about; other labels are yours.
  • Acceptance tests only. Unit tests carry no Allure tags, steps or attachments, so nothing but an acceptance test counts as verification.

docs.title: The commit under test
docs.text:
rdm.pytest_plugin adds, at run time, a commit label to each run of a test that claims a requirement of the spec: the commit under test, with worktree=dirty when the working tree had uncommitted changes. Once per run it also writes Allure's executor.json and environment.properties (who or what ran the tests, and where). environment.properties records worktree=unknown, never clean, when there is no commit to compare against.

Enable the plugin for the acceptance suite only — import its hook in that suite's conftest.py, or pass -p rdm.pytest_plugin --rdm-dhf dhf:

# tests/acceptance/conftest.py
from rdm.pytest_plugin import pytest_runtest_call  # noqa: F401

docs.title: Running the acceptance tests
docs.text:
Run them into a clean results directory (--clean-alluredir, so an earlier run's results never count as evidence), then the gates: the commands are the release gate's. To see one requirement's need, rule, runs and the risks it controls, ask the graph (trace item-01-001 in rdm graph mcp, or rdm graph query). To render the matrix, grouped by user need:

rdm render dhf/documents/traceability_matrix.md dhf/config.yml dhf/data/verification.yml

docs.title: Validation evidence
docs.text: Verification asks whether each requirement is met; validation asks whether each user need is. RDM keeps validation evidence as a record against each user need.

docs.title: Human validation
docs.text: A person's validation judgment is a file in the record, <dhf>/validation/<name>-validation.json, with user_need (the need's id as the spec gives it: a Feature's title, such as Alarms sound), disposition: "approved", reviewer (required: a person makes the judgment) and summary. The release gate names every user need without one, as a warning: a machine cannot supply that judgment, but its absence is never silent.

docs.title: RDM — Design History File
docs.text:
Download as PDF

This is RDM's own DHF: the record RDM keeps about itself, checked by RDM's own gates. Every change lands through a pull request that someone other than its author approves, with the gates green. How RDM works is in the docs (docs/about/how-rdm-works.md); why RDM reads a spec as Gherkin rather than authoring one is ADR 0002 (decisions/).

RDM is not a medical device, so this DHF holds the design-controls slice (requirements, verification, validation, traceability, tool risks), not the full IEC 62304 lifecycle set (a complete risk management file, SOUP register, maintenance and problem-resolution plans, …). rdm gap 62304_2015_class_b over these documents reports those items as missing, as expected.

docs.title: What the record is
docs.text:
Part Where What it holds The spec .pi/spec/<context>/ (outside dhf/; .pi/plan/ links the slices) RDM's requirements and user needs, written the Löyly way: each accepted scenario of spec.feature, stamped @item-NN-SSS, a requirement; each event-model screen, with its Allium surface, a user need The tests tests/acceptance/ each test claims the requirement it verifies with @allure.tag("item-NN-SSS") This directory dhf/ the documents below, and generated evidence 
config.yml                           render configuration
documents/
  verification_and_validation_plan.md how RDM is verified and validated
  architecture.md                    the parts, the bounded contexts and the dependency rule
  design/<context>.md                the design output of one bounded context
  document_control.md                git and GitHub as this record's document control (DC-001, Part 11-mapped)
  tool_validation.md                 RDM's final document (CSV-001, proposed): its validation as a tool,
                                     with its architecture, risk policy and risks, and its whole spec, rendered
  user_manual.md                     the IFU: the docs site's pages, in reading order (IFU-001)
  traceability_matrix.md             the matrix template, rendered from generated data, never hand-edited
decisions/
  adr-0002-…md                       RDM reads a spec as Gherkin and audits it

Generated, never committed (gitignored): dhf/allure-results/ (the acceptance run) and dhf/data/ (the verification data the matrix renders from).

Run the gates as CI does (CLAUDE.md):

uv run pytest tests/acceptance --clean-alluredir --alluredir=dhf/allure-results
uv run rdm story verify --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results -o dhf/data/verification.yml
uv run rdm story release-gate --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results
uv run rdm graph validate --dhf dhf --allure-results dhf/allure-results

Trace a requirement, user need or risk with the trace tool of rdm graph mcp (registered in .mcp.json), or query the record with rdm graph query.

docs.title: docs/ and dhf/
docs.text:
docs/ explains RDM to its users; dhf/ is the record of how RDM itself is designed and verified.

docs/ dhf/ What it is RDM's instructions for use, plus an API reference generated from the docstrings RDM's own design history file Who it's for People and agents using RDM on their own product Whoever governs RDM's development: authors, reviewers, an auditor, and RDM's gates Controlled? Yes, as one document: IFU-001 lists its pages; each change is a reviewed pull request Yes: each change is a reviewed pull request; the release gate requires every requirement verified Checked by mkdocs build --strict, and the tests of the IFU's own requirements The release gate, rdm graph validate, rdm gap Published As the docs site, one copy per release On the same site, each document as a page (and a PDF where Pandoc and Typst run), the spec one page per context, with the traceability matrix and map generated from a live test run

A product that adopts RDM gets its own dhf/ (rdm adopt or rdm init), not RDM's.

docs.title: ADR 0002: RDM reads the spec as Gherkin and audits it with Allure
docs.text:
Download as PDF

Status: Accepted (2026-11-10). It replaces RDM's earlier model, in which RDM held the requirements itself as design inputs.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
RDM used to own the specification. A project wrote design inputs (DI-n in the frontmatter of one design document per bounded context), traced each to a user need registered in the V&V plan, tagged one test per input with @allure.story("DI-n"), and RDM's design gate, scaffolding command and git hooks policed how that record was written.

Software is now increasingly specified and regenerated elsewhere: an agentic factory such as Löyly keeps the specification as stamped Gherkin scenarios, with Allium rules, an event model and an event storm behind them, and rebuilds the code from it. Keeping the same requirement a second time as a design input in RDM makes two hand-kept copies of one fact, which drift.

What a regulated release needs from RDM is not authorship but audit: is every clause of the applicable standards addressed by a document, is every requirement verified by a passing test at the released commit, is every risk controlled, and who approved it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
RDM reads a spec; it never writes it. Its contract with a spec is Gherkin and Allure, and nothing else is fixed.

  • Requirement. A Gherkin scenario tagged with an id is a requirement. By default any id-shaped tag (@REQ-12, @item-02-001) is an id; a spec can name its own pattern. A scenario without one is reported, and blocks a release; so does an id on two scenarios. Feature files are parsed with Cucumber's own parser (gherkin-official).
  • Evidence. A test run claims the requirements it verifies with Allure tag labels naming their ids: what a Gherkin runner writes from a scenario's tags, or @allure.tag("<id>") on a plain test.
  • User need. By default each Gherkin Feature, its description the need's text, addressed by the scenarios under it.
  • Everything else is configuration or an adapter. spec: in the DHF's config.yml names the feature files (globs, exclusions), the id pattern and the needs source; without it RDM looks for spec/ or features/ at the repository root. A layout adapter reads one factory's richer spec: Löyly's (rdm/specification/loyly.py) reads its plan of slices and takes its user needs from the event model's screens, their Allium surfaces and the event storm.
  • What RDM keeps. Gap analysis of documents against compliance checklists; traceability from Allure runs to requirements and user needs; the release gate over requirements, needs, risks and validation records; the knowledge graph and its MCP server; the regulatory documents, the verification report and the evidence bundle.
  • What RDM no longer has. Design inputs and the V&V plan's user-need registry; the design gate, its git hooks and rdm story new-input; source scanning of test tags; and RDM's own process ceremony (design reviews, the agent workflow), which the spec's owner covers in its own process.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One copy of each requirement: changing a scenario changes what the release gate counts, with no second edit.
  • RDM works with any Gherkin spec and any Allure-writing test runner; a factory's richer model is one adapter, not RDM's model.
  • With Features as needs, a scenario addresses exactly one need, the Feature it sits under; a spec that needs a scenario to serve several needs uses an adapter (Löyly's covers them by the Allium rules and guarantees it tags).
  • RDM's own record follows the same model: its spec is written the Löyly way in .pi/ (stamped Given/When/Then scenarios, Allium surfaces, event model, event storm), which rdm init and rdm adopt also lay down for a new spec; its tests claim requirements with @allure.tag("item-NN-SSS"), and its risk controls name requirement ids. Plain Gherkin stays supported: the contract is still only Gherkin and Allure. Against Löyly's spec-v2, the adapter reads 201 requirements, Löyly's own checklist.
  • Breaking for projects on the old model: their design inputs become tagged scenarios, their user needs Features, their story tags Allure tag labels.

docs.title: Evidence is Allure only
docs.text: Graded verdicts (Löyly's sealed graders) are not evidence in RDM: they stay the spec owner's own check. A test run that verifies a requirement writes Allure results, and those alone count. A factory that wants a graded verdict counted turns it into an Allure result tagged with the requirement's id.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: Id: SDS-SYS-001 · Context: system · Kernel: rdm/kernel/ · Composition root: rdm/main.py · References: DC-001 · Download as PDF

docs.title: Bounded contexts
docs.text:
Id Part Layer Code specification Record 2 rdm/specification/ risk Record 1 rdm/risk/ test_evidence Record 3 rdm/evidence/, rdm/pytest_plugin.py release Gates 4 rdm/release/ compliance Gates 1 rdm/compliance/ graph Graph 5 rdm/graph/ publishing Documents 5 rdm/publishing/, rdm/md_extensions/

RDM audits the record of regulated software. It reads a spec as Gherkin (each scenario tagged with an id a requirement), takes the evidence of each requirement from Allure test runs, checks documents against the checklists of the standards that apply, decides whether a release may go ahead, renders regulatory documents, and builds it all into a read-only graph that people and agents query. It never authors the spec (ADR 0002).

This document holds design only: RDM's own requirements and user needs are its spec, written the Löyly way in .pi/ (a slice of .pi/plan/ per bounded context), read like any project's.
