docs.title: The four parts
docs.text:
Part Responsibility Writes to the record? Record read the record: the spec (Gherkin), the risk register, validation records, checklists, test results, git scaffolding only (init, adopt); every other change is a reviewed commit Gates pass/block decisions on the record no Graph the knowledge graph: the record as RDF, queried and validated; agents read it over MCP (rdm graph mcp) no — rebuilt from the record, never edited Documents regulatory documents rendered from the record no

Only people and agents change the record, and only through a reviewed pull request; the merge is the approval. Nothing RDM derives (graph, matrix, documents, evidence bundle) is edited by hand or fed back into the record.

docs.title: System context
docs.text: Who uses RDM: a regulatory author renders documents and checks them against checklists; a team runs the gates in CI on every change; an agent reads the record through the graph's MCP server; a reviewer reads the verification report and the evidence bundle. RDM runs as the rdm command, as a pytest plugin inside a project's acceptance run, and as reusable CI (a GitHub workflow and actions). It depends on git, on Allure results written by the project's test runner, and, to render PDFs, on Pandoc and Typst.

docs.title: Bounded contexts (one design document each), by part
docs.text:
A bounded context is drawn where the language changes, not where the workflow does (CONTEXT.md): the stages of a requirement's life (written, verified, released) are not contexts. The code of each context is in the frontmatter (code).

Part Context Design document Its language Package Record specification (core) design/specification.md spec, slice, scenario, requirement, user need, surface, screen rdm/specification/: the Gherkin reader, the spec's configuration, the Löyly adapter, init, adopt, validation records Record risk design/risk.md hazard, harm, severity, probability, control, residual rdm/risk/ Record test_evidence design/test_evidence.md test run, executor, step, attachment, tag; Allure's words stop here rdm/evidence/: Allure results; and rdm/pytest_plugin.py Gates release design/release.md verified, release gate, finding rdm/release/: the release gate, the verification data; and the reusable CI Gates compliance design/compliance.md standard, checklist, checklist clause, gap, coverage rdm/compliance/ Graph graph design/graph.md knowledge graph, projection, vocabulary, gate rule rdm/graph/: the projection, the shapes, the SPARQL endpoint and the MCP server Documents publishing design/publishing.md template, data, rendered document, evidence bundle rdm/publishing/: render, snippets, DMR index, the verification report, the evidence bundle; and rdm/md_extensions/ and the PDF action

Not contexts: the shared kernel (rdm/kernel/: YAML and file helpers, EDN, ids, git, frontmatter, the reconcile helpers), below every context; and the composition root (rdm/main.py), which wires the command line to every context. Onboarding (init, adopt) is the specification's application layer. Three paths users name stay where they are: rdm/main.py (the rdm command), rdm/pytest_plugin.py (imported by a project's conftest.py) and rdm/md_extensions/ (named in a project's config.yml).

docs.title: Dependency rule
docs.text:
A context imports only contexts of a lower layer, and the shared kernel; nothing imports a context of the top layer. The layers and each context's code are in the frontmatter, and a test fails on any import that breaks the rule, and on any module no context's code holds (tests/dependency_rule_test.py).

 5  publishing · graph              read models: read every context, feed none back
 4  release                         decides: verified status, risk and validation → release
 3  test_evidence                   translates Allure results into runs of the spec's requirements
 2  specification                   the core: the spec read as Gherkin, needs, requirements
 1  risk · compliance               leaves: their own languages, nothing but the kernel
 0  shared kernel                   util · edn · ids · git · frontmatter · reconcile

The leaves sit below the core because the core uses them and they use nothing: the release gate applies the risk rules, and neither leaf reads a requirement. The evidence bundle renders the matrix and the verification report, so it is publishing's, and realises release's item-04-003.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text: The spec → its evidence (Allure runs) and its risks → the release gate decides, and gap analysis holds the documents to their checklists → the knowledge graph and the documents are derived from the same record. Agent skills (how to author requirements, test-first, risk analysis) are maintained outside RDM, in scope-impact/agent-skills. RDM ships no planning tooling: tasks and issues live in their own tools, outside the record (see docs/about/plan-vs-record.md).

docs.title: Not yet in scope
docs.text: In rough order: turning a regulation into a checklist mapped to its standard's clauses; pushing the graph to an external RDF store, with the vocabulary and gate shapes versioned; and several projects in one graph (clause identifiers are already project-independent). Each enters through a user need and requirements in the spec before any code.

docs.title: Compliance — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-GAP-001 · Context: compliance · References: DC-001 · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Compliance holds standards as checklists and checks the controlled documents against them. A checklist is a selection of a standard's clauses, in a plain-text file, that may include other checklists; a checklist clause is one line of it, named by its key; a controlled document references a clause by writing its key inside a [[ … ]] block, such as [[62304:5.1.2]]. A gap is a checklist clause that no document in the set references, and coverage is the share of a checklist's clauses that are referenced. Gap analysis is the activity this context performs (rdm gap); the context itself is named for its domain, compliance with a standard. It knows nothing of requirements, tests or risks: its only inputs are checklists and documents.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Its two components, what each is responsible for, and how they relate:

Component Responsibility Meets Gap analysis Reads a checklist and its includes, finds the clauses no document references, and reports the gaps or the coverage item-05-001, item-05-002, item-05-003 Checklists The built-in checklists, each resolvable by name item-05-002, item-05-004

Gap analysis reads a checklist, named either as a built-in or as a file, and the documents to check, and applies these rules:

  • Reading a checklist. A line's first word is its clause key and the rest its description; a line starting with # is a comment; a line include <name> names a built-in checklist or a file relative to the including one. Each file is read once, told apart by its resolved path, so an include cycle ends and no file is counted twice. A byte-order mark is not part of the first key. A bare include, or a checklist or document that cannot be read, is an error naming it (exit 2).
  • Matching a reference. Only text inside [[ … ]] blocks counts; a bare mention of a key elsewhere is not a reference. A block never runs past a blank line, so a stray [[ does not turn the next paragraphs' mentions into references. Each built-in checklist's keys are unique. A key matches only at key-alphabet boundaries, so a shorter key is never satisfied by a longer sibling (X-1 inside X-12) and a colon-qualified key never satisfies its prefix (FDA-SW inside FDA-SW:sdmp). Two allowances are deliberate: a dotted descendant covers its parent ([[62304:5.6.2.a]] references 62304:5.6.2), and a key may carry an annotation after a colon and a space ([[FDA-SW:sdmp: pointer note]], the idiom the templates of a new project use).
  • Reporting gaps (item-05-001). The missing clauses are printed in checklist format, so the report can itself be used as a checklist, sorted in section order (62304:5.1.2 before 62304:5.1.11), since includes would otherwise scramble the standard's order. The exit status is 3 when any clause is missing, 0 when none is, 1 when no checklist is given, and 2 when the checklist has no clauses: nothing was checked. A document that still holds a placeholder marker is named in a warning, since its references may describe nothing yet.
  • Reporting coverage (item-05-003). For one or more checklists, one table row each (total, missing, covered, percent) and an overall row; in verbose mode, each checklist's missing clauses, the first ten and a count of the rest. It exits as the audit does: 3 when any clause is missing, 2 for a checklist with no clauses or none at all.
  • Listing (item-05-002, item-05-004). The built-in checklists are listed by name.

Checklists holds seventeen built-in checklists (item-05-002): IEC 62304 base lists for classes A, B and C, each including the class below, and the 2006 and 2015 editions of each class, each including that edition's class below and the class's base list; ISO 14971 2007 and 2019; FDA-SW 2005 and 2021 (basic, and enhanced including basic); FDA-CYBER 2018; FDA-HFE 2011; and the 21 CFR Part 11 document-control checklist (item-05-004).

Gap analysis resolves built-in names and follows includes in the Checklists. The knowledge graph's Projection reads checklists and matches checklist references with Gap analysis: it uses the same reading and matching rules, so the graph's clauses and reference links cannot drift from what gap analysis reports. No component of this context uses another context's.

DC-001 is RDM's own document-control statement: git and GitHub as this repository's document control system, each Part 11 clause cited inline. It is a controlled document, not a component; item-05-004's test audits it against the built-in Part 11 checklist.

Assumptions and open questions:

  • The ISO 14971 2019 checklist lists the standard's clauses by number and a short mnemonic title, as the other built-ins do.
  • Verbose coverage names at most ten missing clauses per checklist and counts the rest; the gap report names them all.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Compliance is a leaf, at layer 1 of the dependency rule beside risk: it depends on no other context, not even the specification, since it works on any documents, not on requirements.

Two parts depend on it, both as the rule allows: the composition root, for the rdm gap command, and the knowledge graph (layer 5), a read model above it, for item-06-003 and item-06-009.

docs.title: Knowledge graph — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-GRAPH-001 · Context: graph · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This context owns the knowledge graph: the record — the spec, its test runs, git history, risks and checklists — projected into RDF for people and agents to query, browse and validate. It speaks of projection (one source of the record turned into facts, one named graph per source), the vocabulary (the classes and properties queries and agents rely on: the published language), and gate rules (shapes whose violations block and whose warnings inform). The graph is a read model: it is rebuilt from the spec, the documents and the results on demand, never edited, and never the source of a fact. It is open world: it states only what the record states, so a missing rdm:exercises link means no run claimed the requirement, never unverified; closed-world judgments are the gate rules' and the coded gates'. graph names it in commands and code.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Meets Projection Turns each source of the record into its own named graph, de-duplicated and in a stable order; writes sorted N-Quads; replaces the store on each build; answers SPARQL over the store or an in-memory projection; starts the read-only endpoint; adds checklists on request item-06-001, item-06-002, item-06-003, item-06-008, item-06-009, item-06-011, item-06-012, item-06-013, item-06-014, item-06-015, item-06-016 Vocabulary The classes and properties of the graph; projected as the ontology graph item-06-001 Gate shapes The gate rules as SHACL shapes: violations block exactly what the release gate blocks, warnings inform; plus the checklist data's own shapes item-06-004, item-06-008, item-06-011, item-06-015, item-06-016 SHACL validation rdm graph validate: runs the shipped and any user-supplied shapes over the union of the named graphs, reports each result most severe first, and fails on any violation item-06-010 Explorer file Writes the record as an AWS Graph Explorer file, every record node whatever its IRI, optionally leaving out chosen classes and what hangs only from them item-06-005 Agent server rdm graph mcp: the schema, query, trace and validate tools for agents, read-only, each answering from a projection rebuilt on that call item-06-006, item-06-007, item-06-008, item-06-013

All of them run in the rdm command and need the optional extra graph; without it every rdm graph command exits 2 and names the extra.

How the components relate, in the direction of the arrows:

  • The Projection declares its terms in the Vocabulary, and writes the explorer file with the Explorer file, which takes only the executions graph's name from the Projection, never a second read of the record. It builds the graph store, which the SPARQL endpoint (rdm graph serve) serves read-only to AWS Graph Explorer, its default graph the union of the named graphs, reading the store afresh for each query and refusing what the Agent server refuses.
  • SHACL validation validates the Projection's graph and checks it with the Gate shapes.
  • The Agent server projects the record afresh on each call; validates with SHACL validation; returns the Vocabulary for schema. It never uses the graph store, so an agent never reads a stale graph. The agent harness calls it over MCP stdio; RDM's own repository registers it for its agents.

The behaviour a reviewer needs to judge the design:

  • Named graphs. The record graph holds the spec — its bounded contexts, user needs (text and source; from an adapter, also actors, surfaces, rules, guarantees and storm events), requirements (scenario title, rule, source, the needs they trace to and address) and an adapter's rules — and the controlled documents, each context's declaring document and part, and the documents' references; the executions graph the Allure results, when given; the git graph each document's latest landed commit and the commit the record was built at; the risks graph the register, with a finding about the register as a whole on each risk, or on a stand-in node for the register when it has none; the checklists and references graphs, on request; and the ontology graph the Vocabulary. The traceability matrix template is not projected: it is output, not record.
  • Runs claim requirements. A run's id-shaped Allure tag labels become rdm:exercises links; a claim that names no requirement of the spec is a warning. The executions graph is read with the Allure reader the gates use.
  • Whole-record findings. What the release gate blocks about the record as a whole (no spec, no requirement, an untagged scenario, an id on two scenarios, a spec file or result file that cannot be read) goes on the record's node as the gate words it, and a shape blocks each one, so validation never passes what the gate blocks. A user need is unaddressed when no requirement rdm:addresses it, as the gate decides.
  • Identity. Instance IRIs are urn:dhf:<project>:<kind>/<id>, the project being the repository's name unless another is given, so graphs from several repositories merge without collisions; clause, standard and checklist IRIs (urn:rdm:clause:62304:5.6.2) are project-independent.
  • Vocabulary reuse. Standard terms are reused where they exist: rdm:Requirement rdfs:subClassOf oslc_rm:Requirement (OSLC Requirements Management), Dublin Core for identifiers, titles, descriptions and references, PROV-O for commits, authors and run times, SKOS for checklists. RDM terms (rdm:UserNeed, rdm:BoundedContext, rdm:TestRun, rdm:Risk, rdm:tracesTo, rdm:addresses, rdm:exercises, …) are minted only where none fits; the adapter's terms (rdm:AlliumRule, rdm:coversRule, rdm:facing, …) only when an adapter supplies the facts.
  • What is refused. The Agent server's query, the SPARQL endpoint and rdm graph query refuse SPARQL Update, any SERVICE call outside literals, IRIs and comments (a comment ends at either line break), anything that does not parse as a query, and FROM or FROM NAMED, which would be ignored (a query names a graph with GRAPH); a variable or prefix named SERVICE is not a call. The Agent server's row limit is capped, and every tool is annotated read-only and idempotent. trace answers a requirement (its scenario, rule, needs, runs with their steps and attachments, source files and the risks it controls), a user need or a risk, matched against the ids the record declares and never spliced into a query; anything else is refused. SHACL validation exits 1 on a violation and 2 on a missing DHF or a shapes or checklist file that is missing or not RDF. An --exclude class the graph does not have is refused. The default branch is origin's HEAD, else main or master, else git's init.defaultBranch, else the only local branch.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
A read model at the top layer (5) of the dependency rule: it depends on the contexts below it, and nothing but the composition root depends on it in code; the release context's gates action runs rdm graph validate as a CI step, not as an import. It projects:

  • specification, through the spec reader: contexts, user needs, requirements and an adapter's rules;
  • test evidence, through the Allure reader: results and labels, and the verified set;
  • risk, through the Risk register: the register, the policy, the residual decision and the release gate's findings;
  • compliance, through Gap analysis: the checklist reader, the built-in checklists and the key matcher;
  • release, through the Release gate: its findings about the whole record, which the Projection puts on the record for the shapes;

and the shared kernel (ids, git history, frontmatter). It does not read publishing. No dependency breaks the rule.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Writing back: nothing the graph holds or derives changes the record. Pushing the graph to an external RDF store, versioning the vocabulary and gate shapes, and several projects in one graph are not yet in scope.

docs.title: Publishing — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-REN-001 · Context: publishing · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Publishing renders the record into controlled documents: a template (a controlled document's source, with placeholders) filled with data generated from the record, then post-processed Markdown, and from it PDF and DOCX. It owns the template engine and its filters, the Markdown post-processing, the code snippets a document embeds, the device-master-record (DMR) index data, the verification report and the evidence bundle. Its language is template, data, rendered document and evidence bundle; a rendered document is output, never source. It is a read model: it reads the record through the contexts below it, never changes it, and nothing it renders is fed back into it.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Meets Renderer Fills a template with the data files as its context, each under its file name, in one or two passes, and post-processes the result; refuses a value the data does not supply, and join_to an id its table lacks item-07-001, item-07-002 Markdown extensions Number the sections, give the template the vocabulary the document uses, and remove auditor-only notes item-07-003 First-pass output Holds the words a first render produced, for the second pass to test against item-07-003 Code snippets Collects the delimited snippets of source files, by key, as a data file, refusing a key used twice, in one file or two item-07-004 DMR index Writes one index entry per controlled document from its frontmatter item-07-008 Verification report Builds the report's data from the record and the results it is given, and has it laid out as a PDF item-07-009 Report layout Sets the report's pages, every value as text item-07-009 Evidence bundle Writes the retained release evidence, the verification report among it; refuses a record with no matrix template before writing anything item-04-003, item-07-009 PDF action Renders a repository's documents in the RDM image of the release it is pinned to item-04-004 User manual The instructions for use (IFU): the documentation site's pages (docs/), listed by the controlled document IFU-001 (dhf/documents/user_manual.md) and so in the DMR index; chapters in the order of an IFU, a cover naming its release and revision, and each residual risk disclosed item-07-005, item-07-006, item-07-007 Docs build hooks Publish the DHF pages and draw each traceability map from the graph while the site builds; not part of the manual —

The PDF action is reusable CI; the others run in the rdm command.

The rules a reviewer needs to judge the design:

  • Rendering. A placeholder with no data fails the render rather than rendering empty, with a message naming it (exit 2), as does a template that does not exist; an empty configuration loads no extensions. Each data file is one entry of the template's context, named by the file's name without its extension; two data files with one name are an error. Only when a template asks for the first pass's output is it rendered a second time with that output available; otherwise one pass is the whole render. The filters that build traceability tables are always available to a template.
  • Post-processing. The project's configuration names the Markdown extensions to load, and each runs over the rendered lines in turn. Section numbering prefixes each heading with its number. The vocabulary extension gives the template the words of the first pass, so a glossary or acronym list includes only the terms the document uses. Audit-note exclusion removes each [[…]] note, and the space before it, from the output; a note may run over several lines of one paragraph, and one left open at the paragraph's end is kept as text. Neither extension touches code: fenced blocks (`` or ~~~, also inside a blockquote or a list item) and inline code are left as written, and only an ATX heading (#to######, then a space) is numbered. A project laid down byrdm init` enables only the vocabulary extension.
  • Snippets. A snippet runs from its opening marker to the closing marker in the same column (each a whole word, never part of a longer one), its lines kept from that column. An empty or repeated key in one file, a closing marker in another column, or a missing closing marker is refused, naming the file and line. The snippets are a data file the Renderer reads like any other.
  • DMR index. One entry per Markdown document in the given directory with a frontmatter id (a blank one is none), sorted by id, marked as generated. A document with no id is skipped with a warning; a directory with no controlled document is an error.
  • Verification report. The status of each requirement is the release context's verification data; the report never decides it again. The evidence is release-grade only when no reason is found, and each reason is named: a requirement not verified; a result file that cannot be read; a test that failed or broke; a test run with uncommitted changes, or with no commit; runs of another commit than the product's; a record with uncommitted changes; or a record whose commit is unknown. Every run counts, whether it claims a requirement of the spec or not. The anomalies are a requirement with no run, a run that did not pass, an unreadable result file, a missing attachment and a tag that names no requirement. With no Typst available the report is refused, and the command says so, rather than written without its layout. Because the layout sets every value as text, never markup, nothing a test printed can change the document.
  • Evidence bundle. It holds the verification data, the rendered traceability matrix (when the record has its template), every plain file of the results directory (the results, their attachments, the run's executor and environment; never a symbolic link or anything outside it), so the report's digest over them can be checked after CI's retention ends, the verification report or the reason it was not rendered, and a manifest of the counts, the files this bundle wrote, and each attachment a result names that is missing. A bundle written where one was before replaces the earlier results, never mixes them, and an output that would hold the results directory, or sit inside it, is refused. Neither the bundle nor the report reads a symbolic link in the results directory. It lives here because it renders: the matrix with the Renderer, the report with the Verification report.

The relationships that matter, in the direction of the arrow:

  • The Renderer keeps the first pass's words in the First-pass output and post-processes the rendered Markdown with the Markdown extensions, which give the template the first pass's words from the First-pass output.
  • The Verification report builds on the Verification data (release), reads results with the Allure reader (test evidence), reads the record with the spec reader (specification), reads risk status and residual decisions with the Risk register (risk), and lays out with the Report layout.
  • The DMR index takes each document's frontmatter from the shared kernel.
  • The Evidence bundle writes verification.yml with the Verification data (release), finds the matrix template in the DHF, renders the matrix with the Renderer and writes the report PDF with the Verification report.
  • The Gates action (release) writes the evidence bundle with the Evidence bundle: the one arrow into publishing from another context.
  • The PDF action renders the documents in the Documents image.

Assumptions and open questions:

  • A snippet key repeated across two files is not an error: the later file's snippet silently replaces the earlier one.
  • The DMR index reads only the documents directly in the given directory, not those in its subdirectories (such as the design documents).

docs.title: Order
docs.text: The two passes of a render: the Renderer loads the data files as the template's context, keeps the words of the first pass, and post-processes the Markdown with the extensions, which give the second pass the first pass's words (so a glossary includes only the terms a document uses).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Layer 5 of the dependency rule, a read model: it depends on every context it publishes from — release (the verification data), test_evidence (the Allure reader), specification (the spec reader), risk (the risk register) — and the shared kernel. Within the code, nothing depends on it but the composition root; the release context's Gates action calls the Evidence bundle from reusable CI, as a command, not an import. No dependency breaks the rule.

docs.title: Release — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-REL-001 · Context: release · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: release decides whether a release may go ahead and keeps the evidence it went ahead on: the release gate over the record's verified status, its risks and its user needs; the verification data the gate and its reviewers read; and the reusable gates that run all of it in another repository's pipeline. Its language: a requirement is verified (a passing run claims it, and none that claims it failed); the release gate blocks a release; release-grade evidence is what a release needs; the traceability matrix is generated, never edited; the evidence bundle is what a release keeps. It reads the specification, test evidence and risk; none of them reads it.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Two of the components run in the rdm command, two in the reusable CI that other repositories' pipelines call.

Component Responsibility Meets Release gate The release decision over verified status, risk and validation item-04-001; realises item-01-004, item-02-002, item-02-003 Verification data Every requirement reconciled against the executed results: the data the traceability matrix and the evidence bundle are built from item-04-002, item-04-003 Reusable workflow Runs a repository's acceptance tests, then the gates, with RDM installed from the revision the caller pinned item-04-004 Gates action The gate steps, written once: verification data, release gate, graph validation and the evidence bundle item-04-004, item-04-003

Release gate. It blocks a release when no spec is found, or the spec cannot be read whole (a scenario with no requirement id tag, an id tagging more than one scenario, a file that does not parse); when the spec holds no requirement; when a requirement failed or is untested in the given results; when a result file in them cannot be read (it could hold a failed run); when the risk register's release rules report a blocking finding; and when a user need is addressed by no requirement. It warns, never blocks, on a user need with no approved validation record, and on a claimed tag that looks like a requirement id but names none. A results directory that does not exist is refused.

Verification data. For each requirement: its scenario, rule, source, context, status, run counts, tests and their outputs, grouped under the user needs it addresses (each with its text), with a summary, the tags that match no requirement, and the result files that cannot be read, which make verify exit non-zero. It is generated, never edited.

Reusable workflow and Gates action. The caller pins the workflow and names the same revision again as an input, because a reusable workflow cannot see the revision it was called at. The workflow checks out the caller's repository with its history and RDM at that revision, installs RDM and the test tools from that checkout (never from a package index), runs the caller's acceptance tests, then the Gates action, and uploads the Allure report and the verification record. The Gates action installs RDM from its own revision unless the caller already has; each gate can be switched off for a record that is not yet ready for it; the verification data and the evidence bundle run only when there are results, and the bundle is uploaded for retention. Inputs reach the steps' scripts as environment variables, never spliced into the script text, so an input cannot inject shell.

Relationships that matter, in the direction of the arrow:

  • The release gate reads the spec and the validation records (specification), reconciles results with the Allure reader (test_evidence) and reports the risk findings of the risk register (risk).
  • Verification data reconciles results with the Allure reader and reads the spec.
  • The Reusable workflow runs the acceptance test run and then the gates with the Gates action, which writes the verification data, runs the release gate, validates the graph with SHACL validation (graph) and writes the evidence bundle with the Evidence bundle (publishing).

The release gate does not decide whether the runs are release-grade evidence (the commit and worktree each run tested): the verification report and, as a warning, the knowledge graph's gate shapes show it.

docs.title: Order
docs.text: The order of a pipeline run matters: the acceptance tests write the Allure results; the verification data is written; the release gate decides; graph validation runs; the evidence bundle is written last, from the same results, and uploaded.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Layer 4 of the dependency rule. Depends on test_evidence (the Allure reader), specification (the spec, the validation records) and risk (the risk register), all below it, and on the shared kernel. Depended on by publishing (the verification report and the evidence bundle build on the verification data) and by the composition root. The Gates action also runs graph's SHACL validation and publishing's evidence bundle as commands; that is a run, not an import, so the rule is not broken.

docs.title: Risk — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-RISK-001 · Context: risk · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This context owns the risk register as part of the record, and the risk acceptability criteria the register is evaluated against. Its language is risk analysis and risk evaluation: a risk is a hazard, the hazardous situation it leads to and the harm that situation can cause — one harm pathway per risk — with a severity from the harm and a probability from the situation; a safety risk or a STRIDE threat; the risk controls that reduce it, each a requirement; the initial risk and the residual risk, the same estimate before and after the controls; and a proposal, a rating or a policy no person has approved yet. The method (hazard → situation → harm; evaluate, control, verify, evaluate again) is the team's; this context keeps the register and checks what a machine can check.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Its one component, and how the components of other contexts use it:

Component Responsibility Meets Risk register Reads the declared risk policy (refusing a second) and the register, evaluates each risk's initial and residual risk against the policy, gives each risk its residual decision, and writes the risk rules as findings, each blocking or a warning and tied to the risk it is about item-02-001, item-02-002, item-02-003

The register is the frontmatter of kind: risk documents — the record interface authors write, with one entry per risk:

risks:
  - id: RISK-TOOL-001
    category: safety             # or security, with stride:
    linked: [RISK-TOOL-002]      # optional: risks it bears on
    hazard: "What could go wrong, and the sequence of events"
    situation: "The hazardous situation"
    harm: "Who is hurt, and how"
    severity: Serious            # from the harm
    probability: Possible        # from the situation
    level: Medium                # optional; must be the policy's level
    controls: [item-04-001]      # each control is a requirement of the spec
    residual: {probability: Rare}  # severity optional: the initial's
    acceptance: {by: "...", rationale: "..."}
    status: proposed             # until a person approves the rating

The rules the Risk register applies, which a reviewer needs to judge it:

  • The policy. The project declares at most one risk policy (a risk_policy in the frontmatter of a record document; the first by path is the one read). A policy that does not give a level for every pair, or an acceptability for every level, is one blocking finding naming its document, and the register is not checked further until it is fixed. The policy's status is its document's; an unapproved policy is a warning. A policy that lists a severity or a probability twice is malformed: one pair would have two levels.
  • Evaluation. With no policy no risk is evaluated, and a register with risks blocks. A risk with no controls keeps its initial risk as its residual risk, whatever residual it declares: only a control reduces a risk. A hazard, situation or harm is text; anything else is empty. A control or a link written as one value, not a list, is that one value. The policy's severities may be numbers as well as names. A risk's status is its own, else its document's, else proposed: no status is never read as approved. A risk id is text or a number; anything else is no id. A recorded level, initial or residual, must be the policy's.
  • The residual decision is one of: not evaluated (no policy, no residual level, or a control without a passing test), acceptable, accepted (a level the policy accepts only with justification, with who accepted it and why, both text), needs acceptance, or unacceptable. Only acceptable and accepted let a release through.
  • The register. A document of kind risk (in any case) holds its risks as a list of mappings under risks; any other shape, or no risks at all, is a blocking finding naming the document, never a register silently left out. A document that only declares the risk policy is not a register.
  • The findings are every refusal of item-02-002 and item-02-003, and also a risk whose status is neither proposed nor approved, which blocks. A proposed risk or policy is a warning. The Risk register is the one place these rules are written.

Relationships, in the direction of the arrow:

  • The Release gate (release) reports the risk findings of the Risk register: it adds the blocking findings to its blocking list and the warnings to its warnings: the part of item-02-002 and item-02-003 the release context applies.
  • The Projection (graph) reads risks and findings with the Risk register — the policy, the register, each residual decision and the findings — into the risks named graph for its gate shapes (item-06-008, owned by graph), so the release gate and the shapes cannot disagree.
  • The Verification report (publishing) reads risk status and residual decisions with the Risk register, beside the requirements that control each risk.

The Risk register is handed the requirement ids and the verified ones; it reads nothing of the spec itself. It parses frontmatter with the shared kernel.

Assumption: one harm pathway per risk, with one probability; no control effect is recorded apart — the residual is all the controls folded together. The register is kept this small; each can grow later without changing a register written to this format.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Layer 1 of the dependency rule, a leaf: it depends only on the shared kernel, and on no other context. The contexts that use it sit above it: release (the release gate), publishing (the verification report) and graph (the projection).

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text: Whether a risk control is effective is shown in the record only as far as a machine can see it: the control is verified and the risk, evaluated again, has an acceptable or accepted residual. Whether the control does what it claims in the code, whether the rating is right, and whether a residual is as low as reasonably practicable stay human judgements, made in review and recorded by approving the rating (status: approved).

docs.title: Specification — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-SPEC-001 · Context: specification · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The core bounded context: the spec the record is held to, read and never written. RDM's contract with a spec is Gherkin: a requirement is a scenario tagged with an id, and a user need is, by default, a Feature. Where the feature files are, what an id looks like and where user needs come from are the DHF's configuration (spec: in config.yml), or an adapter for one layout (Löyly's). Every other context conforms to its ids. It also reads the validation records of the user needs. Onboarding (rdm init, rdm adopt), the commands that lay a project down, is this context's application layer.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Meets Gherkin reader Parses feature files with Cucumber's Gherkin parser: each scenario (or outline) tagged with an id (any id-shaped tag, or the configured pattern) is a requirement, with its Feature, Rule, title, source line and tags; the last id tag of a scenario is its id; each untagged scenario is listed; a file that does not parse is a problem, never skipped. item-01-001 Spec configuration Finds the spec the record is held to (spec in the DHF's config.yml: feature globs, exclusions, id pattern, needs source, layout; else .pi/plan, spec/ or features/ from the repository root) and its user needs: by default each Feature, addressed by the scenarios under it. item-01-001, item-01-005 Löyly adapter An optional layout and needs source: Löyly's plan of slices (planned and backlog skipped, drafts.feature never read) and its user needs, the event-model screens with their Allium surfaces, actors, rules and guarantees and the event-storm events behind them. item-01-001, item-01-005 Project scaffold rdm init: copies the project templates into a new directory; refuses a directory that exists (exit 2), and on success names what it laid down and the next steps. item-01-002 Project templates What rdm init lays down: the document templates (the traceability matrix among them), the build Makefile (a Word document is rebuilt when its reference document changes), the render configuration, the container build (installing the RDM release from git when no wheel is given), and the Pandoc and Typst configuration. Templates use only local images. item-01-002 Adoption rdm adopt: creates each missing file of the adoption templates and skips, never overwrites, one that exists (a symbolic link exists, dangling or not); when a .gitignore exists, names the lines of RDM's generated files to add to it; stamps the installed version as its release tag (a pre-release such as 2.0.0a0 as 2.0.0-alpha, the tag the release and its image carry); reports what it skipped and prints the next steps. item-01-003 Adoption templates What rdm adopt lays down: the DHF skeleton (V&V plan, traceability matrix, render configuration, README), a CI gate workflow and a .gitignore of RDM's generated files (Allure results, verification data, the graph store, bytecode). item-01-003 Validation records Reads the validation records from the DHF's validation directory, each naming a user need by its id; only an approved disposition with a named reviewer counts. Gives the user needs without one. item-01-004
  • The Gherkin reader reads every feature file the spec configuration finds, or that the Löyly adapter's layout lists.
  • The spec configuration takes its user needs from the Features, or hands the context directories to the Löyly adapter for its needs.
  • Validation records read the user needs from the spec.
  • Project scaffold and adoption copy their templates.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Layer 2 of the dependency rule. Depends on the shared kernel only (YAML, EDN for the adapter) and on Cucumber's Gherkin parser. Depended on by test_evidence (the pytest plugin reads the requirement ids), release (the release gate, the verification data), publishing (the DMR index, the verification report, the evidence bundle) and graph (the projection). The composition root wires its commands. It reads no results and no risk register.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Writing or stamping the spec: whoever owns it does (ADR 0002).
  • Usability validation by simulated users: the human validation record is the evidence.
  • Planning: tasks and issues live outside the record.

docs.title: Test evidence — Software Design
docs.text: Id: SDS-EVID-001 · Context: test_evidence · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: This context takes Allure results and turns them into evidence about the spec's requirements. Its language is the test run (one execution of a test, at one commit, by one executor), the executor (the CI job or the machine that ran it), the step (a verification step, with its own result), the attachment (what a run kept) and the tag (a run's claim on a requirement, by its id). Allure's words (result, label, container) are read and written here and stop at its boundary.

docs.title: Design Outputs
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Meets Allure reader Reads each result as a test run: its name, its test (file, class and function, from Allure's full name), its result, the requirements its tag labels claim, the outputs it labels, its commit; gives each requirement its status. A result it cannot read is named, never skipped. item-03-001; realises item-04-002 pytest plugin Labels each run of a test that claims a requirement of the spec with the commit under test and, when the working tree had uncommitted changes, marks it; records the executor and environment once per run item-03-002, item-03-003

Allure reader. A run claims a requirement with a tag label naming its id: a Gherkin runner writes the scenario's tags as such labels, and a plain test writes @allure.tag("<id>"); a leading @ is dropped. A run whose step failed or broke has failed, whatever its own status says. A result it cannot read is named and could hold a failed run: not JSON, not an object, not UTF-8, nested too deep, a symbolic link, a status Allure does not write, or labels that are not name and value text. Its reconciliation gives each requirement failed when any of its runs failed or broke, else verified when any passed, else untested; a claimed id that is no requirement is an orphan, reported when it shares a requirement id's leading letters (a mistyped Item_01_001), and an unrelated tag (smoke) is left alone.

pytest plugin. It runs inside the acceptance test run, not in rdm, and acts only on a test whose @allure.tag(...) names a requirement of the spec. It adds no requirement labels: the test's own tag is the claim. It labels the run with the commit under test and the worktree state (unknown when there is no commit), and once per run, when the run writes Allure results, records the executor (a CI run with its run and URL, a local run with its user and host) and the environment (operating system, Python, pytest, allure-pytest and RDM versions, commit, worktree, CI details).

The release gate, the verification data, the verification report and the projection read results with the Allure reader. The plugin reads the requirement ids with the specification's reader.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Layer 3 of the dependency rule. Depends on specification (the plugin reads the requirement ids) and the shared kernel, both below it. Depended on by release (the release gate, the verification data), publishing (the verification report) and graph (the projection).

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Test-result formats other than Allure: a runner that writes another format needs an Allure adapter of its own.
  • Code coverage: a unit-test measure, never acceptance evidence.

docs.title: Document Control — git as the document control system for RDM's record
docs.text: Id: DC-001 · Revision: 5 · Download as PDF

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: States how the controlled records in RDM's repository are controlled: RDM's own — this Design History File, its computer software validation (CSV-001), its spec (.pi/spec/), its tests and the source that meets them — and the worked example's, the computer software validation of Löyly's pi harness (examples/loyly-pi-harness/, CSV-HAR-001). This is the one Part 11 document for both: they share this repository, its history and its review. RDM keeps its record in git, with GitHub as the service provider; this statement maps each applicable 21 CFR Part 11 control to the mechanism that meets it, and it must pass gap analysis against RDM's own shipped part11_document_control checklist (item-05-004 — the same checklist any downstream project audits with is the one this record is held to).

docs.title: The system
docs.text: The master copy of every controlled record is the repository's default branch. Drafts are branches; review and approval happen on the pull request; releases are tags; the revision history is the git history itself. Planning artifacts (tasks, issues) are coordination, never part of the record (docs/about/plan-vs-record.md).

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Validation [[P11:11.10a]] — RDM and this record system are validated as CSV-001 records (computer software assurance, on a documented risk assessment). The controls are enforced configuration and code, exercised on every change: the CI pipeline (design-controls.yml) and the branch ruleset run RDM's own release gate and graph validation, verified by RDM's own acceptance tests, with every change independently reviewed on its pull request. Altered records are discernible by construction — any change produces a new SHA.
  • Copies [[P11:11.10b]] — accurate and complete copies in human-readable and electronic form: the rendered documentation site and the rendered traceability matrix are generated from the record by rdm render; a git archive at any tag reproduces the complete electronic record set.
  • Retention and retrieval [[P11:11.10c]] — every clone is a full replica of the history; release tags identify record baselines; the GitHub-hosted repository is the retained store. Retention period: the full history is retained for as long as RDM is maintained, and release baselines (tags and their evidence bundles) for no less than five years after the release they record. An organization-controlled mirror is an open action (audit NC-6).
  • Access [[P11:11.10d]] — write access is limited to authorized individuals through GitHub organization membership with two-factor authentication; the audit log records permission changes.
  • Device checks [[P11:11.10h]] — every writing client is authenticated to an account-bound credential (SSH key or token issued to the individual's 2FA-protected account); anonymous or unauthenticated input cannot reach the record.
  • Signature accountability [[P11:11.10j]] — the contributor policy (AGENTS.md and this statement, both controlled documents) states that a pull-request approval is the approver's electronic signature and that the approver is accountable for what it approves; the approver is named on the pull request.
  • Audit trail [[P11:11.10e]] — the git history: secure (SHA-chained), computer-generated, time-stamped, author-attributed on every action; a later change never obscures an earlier entry, and the trail lives exactly as long as the record it belongs to.
  • Sequencing [[P11:11.10f]] — the enforced order of steps: CI blocks merge until the acceptance tests, verification, the release gate and graph validation pass, in that order; the reviewer of each pull request checks a requirement's scenario is in the spec before the code that meets it.
  • Authority [[P11:11.10g]] — only authorized reviewers can approve a pull request into the default branch, and the approver must not be the change's author (enforced by the ruleset's required review). The branch controls are configuration code in this repository — .github/rulesets/controlled-record.json (pull-request review, verified commit signatures, required checks, no history rewriting) and repo-settings.json — applied and drift-checked with scripts/apply-repo-controls.sh [--check].
  • Training [[P11:11.10i]] — contributors (human or agent) are directed through AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md before changing the record; agent sessions load them at session start.
  • Systems documentation control [[P11:11.10k]] — this statement, the contributor guide and the CI workflow are themselves version-controlled in this repository and change only through the same approved path they describe.
  • Signature manifestation [[P11:11.50]] — the pull-request review records the approver, the UTC timestamp, and the meaning of the signing (APPROVED — reviewed and approved for the record); the merged, reviewed PR is RDM's approval record by design (no duplicate sign-off blocks exist in the DHF).
  • Signature–record linking [[P11:11.70]] — a review is bound to the exact commit SHA it approves; content-addressing makes a signature inseparable from what was signed.
  • Signature uniqueness [[P11:11.100]] — one GitHub account per individual, two-factor authentication, accounts never reused or reassigned.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: rdm gap part11_document_control dhf/documents/document_control.md must exit zero; the item-05-004 acceptance test executes exactly that, so this statement can never silently drop a control.

docs.title: Computer software validation — RDM
docs.text:
Id: CSV-001 · Status: proposed · References: VVP-001, DC-001, SDS-SYS-001 · Kind: risk · Download as PDF

Proposed, not yet approved. The validation of RDM as a tool: software used as part of a regulated team's quality management system, not a medical device, validated the computer software assurance way, risk based ([[13485:4.1.6-procedure]]). This is RDM's final document: its intended use, its architecture, its risk analysis (the risk policy and the risks are this document's frontmatter, which the release gate evaluates), its whole spec with each requirement's verification, the assurance, the record and change. It is a template: rdm render fills in the architecture and the spec from the record, with the include and glob filters, and the verification from data/verification.yml. A team that adopts RDM validates it for its own intended use; this record is the supplier's assurance it can rely on.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text: RDM reads a team's spec, checklists, risks, documents and executed test results; reports the checklist clauses no document references (gap analysis); decides whether a release may go ahead (the release gate); and generates the verification report and the evidence bundle, which are quality records. It is used directly as part of the quality management system: it automates a quality process (the release decision) and maintains quality records ([[CSA:intended-use]]). It does not produce the product itself, so ISO 13485 7.5.6 applies to it only where a team uses its gates inside production.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
RDM audits the record of regulated software. It reads a spec as Gherkin (each scenario tagged with an id a requirement), takes the evidence of each requirement from Allure test runs, checks documents against the checklists of the standards that apply, decides whether a release may go ahead, renders regulatory documents, and builds it all into a read-only graph that people and agents query. It never authors the spec (ADR 0002).

This document holds design only: RDM's own requirements and user needs are its spec, written the Löyly way in .pi/ (a slice of .pi/plan/ per bounded context), read like any project's.

docs.title: Context map
docs.text:
Each bounded context in its part; an arrow is a dependency in the code (the context imports the one it points to), downwards only, as the dependency rule requires (below).

docs.title: The four parts
docs.text:
Part Responsibility Writes to the record? Record read the record: the spec (Gherkin), the risk register, validation records, checklists, test results, git scaffolding only (init, adopt); every other change is a reviewed commit Gates pass/block decisions on the record no Graph the knowledge graph: the record as RDF, queried and validated; agents read it over MCP (rdm graph mcp) no — rebuilt from the record, never edited Documents regulatory documents rendered from the record no

Only people and agents change the record, and only through a reviewed pull request; the merge is the approval. Nothing RDM derives (graph, matrix, documents, evidence bundle) is edited by hand or fed back into the record.

docs.title: System context
docs.text: Who uses RDM: a regulatory author renders documents and checks them against checklists; a team runs the gates in CI on every change; an agent reads the record through the graph's MCP server; a reviewer reads the verification report and the evidence bundle. RDM runs as the rdm command, as a pytest plugin inside a project's acceptance run, and as reusable CI (a GitHub workflow and actions). It depends on git, on Allure results written by the project's test runner, and, to render PDFs, on Pandoc and Typst.

docs.title: Bounded contexts (one design document each), by part
docs.text:
A bounded context is drawn where the language changes, not where the workflow does (CONTEXT.md): the stages of a requirement's life (written, verified, released) are not contexts. The code of each context is in the frontmatter (code).

Part Context Design document Its language Package Record specification (core) design/specification.md spec, slice, scenario, requirement, user need, surface, screen rdm/specification/: the Gherkin reader, the spec's configuration, the Löyly adapter, init, adopt, validation records Record risk design/risk.md hazard, harm, severity, probability, control, residual rdm/risk/ Record test_evidence design/test_evidence.md test run, executor, step, attachment, tag; Allure's words stop here rdm/evidence/: Allure results; and rdm/pytest_plugin.py Gates release design/release.md verified, release gate, finding rdm/release/: the release gate, the verification data; and the reusable CI Gates compliance design/compliance.md standard, checklist, checklist clause, gap, coverage rdm/compliance/ Graph graph design/graph.md knowledge graph, projection, vocabulary, gate rule rdm/graph/: the projection, the shapes, the SPARQL endpoint and the MCP server Documents publishing design/publishing.md template, data, rendered document, evidence bundle rdm/publishing/: render, snippets, DMR index, the verification report, the evidence bundle; and rdm/md_extensions/ and the PDF action

Not contexts: the shared kernel (rdm/kernel/: YAML and file helpers, EDN, ids, git, frontmatter, the reconcile helpers), below every context; and the composition root (rdm/main.py), which wires the command line to every context. Onboarding (init, adopt) is the specification's application layer. Three paths users name stay where they are: rdm/main.py (the rdm command), rdm/pytest_plugin.py (imported by a project's conftest.py) and rdm/md_extensions/ (named in a project's config.yml).

docs.title: Dependency rule
docs.text:
A context imports only contexts of a lower layer, and the shared kernel; nothing imports a context of the top layer. The layers and each context's code are in the frontmatter, and a test fails on any import that breaks the rule, and on any module no context's code holds (tests/dependency_rule_test.py).

 5  publishing · graph              read models: read every context, feed none back
 4  release                         decides: verified status, risk and validation → release
 3  test_evidence                   translates Allure results into runs of the spec's requirements
 2  specification                   the core: the spec read as Gherkin, needs, requirements
 1  risk · compliance               leaves: their own languages, nothing but the kernel
 0  shared kernel                   util · edn · ids · git · frontmatter · reconcile

The leaves sit below the core because the core uses them and they use nothing: the release gate applies the risk rules, and neither leaf reads a requirement. The evidence bundle renders the matrix and the verification report, so it is publishing's, and realises release's item-04-003.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text: The spec → its evidence (Allure runs) and its risks → the release gate decides, and gap analysis holds the documents to their checklists → the knowledge graph and the documents are derived from the same record. Agent skills (how to author requirements, test-first, risk analysis) are maintained outside RDM, in scope-impact/agent-skills. RDM ships no planning tooling: tasks and issues live in their own tools, outside the record (see docs/about/plan-vs-record.md).

docs.title: Not yet in scope
docs.text: In rough order: turning a regulation into a checklist mapped to its standard's clauses; pushing the graph to an external RDF store, with the vocabulary and gate shapes versioned; and several projects in one graph (clause identifiers are already project-independent). Each enters through a user need and requirements in the spec before any code.

docs.title: Process risk
docs.text:
A failure of RDM to perform as intended could let a release go ahead with a requirement not verified, a risk not evaluated, or evidence that does not describe what was tested: RDM determines acceptability with limited additional human review where a team relies on its gate alone. That is a quality problem that could foreseeably compromise safety: high process risk ([[CSA:risk]], [[13485:4.1.6-proportionate]]). The ways it could fail are the risks below, evaluated against the risk policy below (severity from the harm, probability from the situation, the residual after the controls), each control a requirement of RDM's own spec. The analysis covers every factor the guidance names (its §V.A(2)), for failures that are reasonably foreseeable, not only likely:

Factor Risks Configuration and management RISK-TOOL-008 (the spec read short) Security RISK-TOOL-004, RISK-TOOL-006, RISK-TOOL-007 Data integrity RISK-TOOL-002, RISK-TOOL-005 Data storage RISK-TOOL-009 (evidence not retrievable) Data transfer, operation error RISK-TOOL-010 (a decision on other results)

docs.title: Risk policy
docs.text:
Severity / probability Rare Unlikely Possible Likely Critical Medium High High Block Serious Low Medium High High Minor Low Low Medium Medium Negligible Low Low Low Low
  • Low — acceptable
  • Medium — justify
  • High — justify
  • Block — unacceptable

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
Risk Hazard Before After Decision RISK-TOOL-002 The release gate passes a requirement whose test failed or never ran. High Low acceptable RISK-TOOL-004 An agent changes the controlled record through RDM without review. High Low acceptable RISK-TOOL-005 A test that claims a requirement passes without checking everything its scenario states. High High accepted RISK-TOOL-006 The served graph accepts SPARQL updates from any web origin. Medium Low acceptable RISK-TOOL-007 A read-only query can make RDM send network requests. Medium Low acceptable RISK-TOOL-008 The spec is read short: requirements are left out and no one notices. High Low acceptable RISK-TOOL-009 The evidence that a release was verified cannot be retrieved later. Medium Medium accepted RISK-TOOL-010 The gate decides on results that are not the evidence of the commit being released. Medium Low acceptable

RISK-TOOL-002 safety proposed High → Low

Hazard The release gate passes a requirement whose test failed or never ran. Situation A test fails, errors or is skipped in CI, and the release gate still reports PASSED. Harm A team releases software with a requirement that is not verified. Rating Serious × Possible = High; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-04-001 The release gate passes only when every requirement has a passing run and none fails ✓ verified
  • item-04-002 Verified, failed and untested come from the runs that carry each requirement's id ✓ verified

RISK-TOOL-004 security Tampering proposed High → Low

Hazard An agent changes the controlled record through RDM without review. Situation An agent connected to rdm graph mcp issues a SPARQL Update or looks for a write tool. Harm The record diverges from what reviewers approved, and evidence no one reviewed is presented as controlled. Rating Serious × Possible = High; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-06-007 The agent server cannot change the record or reach the network ✓ verified

RISK-TOOL-005 safety proposed High → High

Hazard A test that claims a requirement passes without checking everything its scenario states. Situation A test checks two of the three things a requirement requires, and the pull-request reviewer does not notice. Harm The requirement is reported verified while one thing it requires is unchecked, and the gap ships. Rating Serious × Possible = High; after its controls Serious × Possible = High: accepted

Controls none

Accepted by RDM maintainers, by approving the pull request that records this register: Whether a test proves its requirement is a reviewer's judgement, made in the pull-request review; no gate can make it. Monitored by reviewers reading each changed test against its scenario's text.

RISK-TOOL-006 security Tampering proposed Medium → Low

Hazard The served graph accepts SPARQL updates from any web origin. Situation A person browses the graph in Graph Explorer while a web page they have open posts an update to the local endpoint. Harm The graph the person reviews is cleared or shows forged verification, and they act on evidence the record does not hold. Rating Serious × Unlikely = Medium; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-06-002 The store is replaced on each build, queried with SPARQL and served read-only ✓ verified

RISK-TOOL-007 security Information disclosure proposed Medium → Low

Hazard A read-only query can make RDM send network requests. Situation A prompt-injected agent, or a web page posting to the served endpoint, sends a query with a SERVICE clause naming an internal or external address. Harm The server probes or reaches services from the user's machine, outside the review the record is under. Rating Serious × Unlikely = Medium; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-06-007 The agent server cannot change the record or reach the network ✓ verified
  • item-06-002 The store is replaced on each build, queried with SPARQL and served read-only ✓ verified

RISK-TOOL-008 safety proposed High → Low

Hazard The spec is read short: requirements are left out and no one notices. Situation A context's spec is missing from the repository (ignored by git, or a plan link to a folder never committed), and the gate counts only what it found. Harm A release passes with requirements that were never checked, reported as complete. Rating Serious × Possible = High; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-04-001 The release gate passes only when every requirement has a passing run and none fails ✓ verified
  • item-01-001 Every tagged scenario is a requirement, wherever the spec's layout keeps it ✓ verified

RISK-TOOL-009 safety proposed Medium → Medium

Hazard The evidence that a release was verified cannot be retrieved later. Situation The CI artifact holding the evidence bundle expires, or the repository is lost. Harm An auditor cannot confirm what was verified for a release, and the team cannot show it. Rating Serious × Unlikely = Medium; after its controls Serious × Unlikely = Medium: accepted

Controls

  • item-04-003 The evidence bundle holds the verification data, the rendered matrix, the report and the results ✓ verified

Accepted by RDM maintainers, by approving the pull request that records this register: RDM writes the complete, checksummed bundle; keeping it for the retention period is document control's job (DC-001, 11.10(c)), not the tool's. Monitored through DC-001's retention commitment.

RISK-TOOL-010 safety proposed Medium → Low

Hazard The gate decides on results that are not the evidence of the commit being released. Situation Results are altered or swapped on their way from the test job to the gate, or an earlier run's results are used. Harm A release is approved on evidence of something else. Rating Serious × Unlikely = Medium; after its controls Serious × Rare = Low: acceptable

Controls

  • item-06-016 Each run links to the commit it tested, and a run of another commit than the product's is stale ✓ verified
  • item-07-009 The verification report shows a reviewer who did not run the tests what was verified ✓ verified
  • item-04-003 The evidence bundle holds the verification data, the rendered matrix, the report and the results ✓ verified

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
RDM's spec, written the Löyly way in .pi/spec/: each accepted scenario, a concrete Given/When/Then example stamped @item-NN-SSS, is a requirement, verified by the acceptance test that claims it; each event-model screen, linked to its Allium surface, is a user need. The table is each requirement's verification from the executed results; the feature files follow, laid out by the gherkin render filter.

The spec was written after RDM's code, to describe it, so for this revision only the Gherkin is held to the code, by the tests that claim it; the Allium surfaces and event models are held to it by review. From the next change on, RDM is built the Löyly way, spec first and then regenerated, so the code cannot drift from any part of the spec.
